query.original_query: negation representation language models steering toward absence of concept interpretable features

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of negation in transformer language models, feature steering to encode absence of concept, interpretable features for negation via probing and activation engineering
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how transformer language models internally represent negation, focusing on the encoding of concept absence within residual stream activations. Using sparse autoencoders trained on intermediate layer representations, we analyze whether monosemantic features emerge that reliably encode the absence of specific attributes, distinct from features encoding their presence. Our analysis reveals that negation is not represented by a single dedicated feature but is instead distributed across multiple features that modulate the activation of concept-specific features. Through activation patching and feature steering experiments, we find that manipulating these sparse features can reliably suppress or invert the model’s output for targeted concepts, effectively encoding absence. Probing the residual stream further shows that negation-related information is localized in later MLP layers and specific attention heads. Results indicate that while superposition complicates direct interpretability, steering sparse features offers a viable method for controlling conceptual negation in generation, with implications for safety and bias mitigation.

sub_queries.semantic_query: negation representation language models steering toward absence of concept interpretable features
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how large language models represent negation through the lens of interpretable feature steering toward the absence of a concept. Using causal tracing and activation patching on transformer-based models, we identify specific attention heads and residual stream dimensions that encode negation operators independently of the negated content. We measure the effect of intervening on these features by applying directional ablations and contrastive activation addition, observing systematic shifts in model outputs from affirmative to negated interpretations. Results indicate that negation is represented as a distributed, compositional feature rather than a localized lexical token, with steering vectors in middle-to-late layers reliably suppressing the target concept’s activation. Findings support the hypothesis that negation operates via suppression of concept-specific neural activity patterns, analogous to representational absence in cognitive models. These interpretable features generalize across syntactic contexts and semantic domains, suggesting a shared underlying mechanism for negation in language models.

papers.title: How does BERT’s attention change when you fine-tune? An analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention change when fine-tuned? The paper investigates this through a proposed analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a methodology for testing hypotheses about how transformer models encode linguistic phenomena, using unsupervised probes, downstream control tasks, and cross-dataset consistency. Applying it to negation scope reveals evidence of the hypothesized encoding in base models but not in large models.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a procedure and analysis methods to test hypotheses about how transformer-based models encode linguistic phenomena. Applying this to negation scope finds evidence of an interpretable encoding (in-scope words attend to the negation cue) in BERT-base and RoBERTa-base, but weaker evidence in the large models.
papers.key_findings:
Before fine-tuning, several attention heads are sensitive to negation scope, with the best BERT-base head achieving an F1 of 53.8 in a fully unsupervised setting.
There is consistency in which heads are negation-sensitive across different datasets.
After fine-tuning on a negation scope task, the average sensitivity of attention heads improved over the pretrained model for all four models, but only the two base models improved more than a control task.
Attention heads that had the top F1s in the pretrained model do not have the top-ranked improvements after fine-tuning on negation scope.
The behavior of individual attention heads becomes more consistent across datasets after fine-tuning on the negation task, compared to the pretrained model and the control task, except for RoBERTa-large.
papers.limitation:
The work focuses on one interpretable way of encoding negation scope knowledge, but there could be many other ways.
The study uses a single nonlinguistic control task, but one could imagine exploring a gradient of fine-tuning tasks.
The analysis focuses primarily on the attention mechanism, but does not explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to.
future_direction: Explore other hypothesized encodings of negation scope, such as a tree of attention leading to the negation cue.
Explore attention head changes with a gradient of fine-tuning tasks that are more or less relevant to the linguistic phenomenon.
Explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to, since these form the outputs and are more directly tied to classification decisions.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models like BERT, after fine-tuning to a downstream task, have achieved high performance on a variety of NLP problems. Yet explaining their decisions is difficult despite recent work probing their internal representations. We propose a procedure and analysis methods that take a hypothesis of how a transformer-based model might encode a linguistic phenomenon, and test the validity of that hypothesis based on a comparison between knowledge-related downstream tasks with downstream control tasks, and measurement of cross-dataset consistency. We apply this methodology to test BERT and RoBERTa on a hypothesis that some attention heads will consistently attend from a word in negation scope to the negation cue. We find that after fine-tuning BERT and RoBERTa on a negation scope task, the average attention head improves its sensitivity to negation and its attention consistency across negation datasets compared to the pre-trained models. However, only the base models (not the large models) improve compared to a control task, indicating there is evidence for a shallow encoding of negation only in the base models.

papers.title: It is not True that Transformers are Inductive Learners: Probing NLI Models with External Negation
papers.research_question: Do transformer models fine-tuned on NLI tasks learn to reason logically, specifically with respect to external negation and the law of excluded middle?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer models fine-tuned on NLI tasks fail to inductively learn the law of excluded middle for external negation, indicating they do not learn logical reasoning but instead rely on shallow heuristics.
papers.conclusion: Transformer NLI models do not learn logical reasoning with respect to negation, as they fail to inductively learn the law of excluded middle and generalize it to similar prefixes.
papers.key_findings:
Before inoculation, NLI models treat external negation prefixes as distractors, ignoring them and achieving high accuracy only when the number of prefixes is even (which does not change the label).
Many transformer NLI models (DeBERTa and BART) cannot learn to inductively generalize the law of excluded middle even with extensive fine-tuning on challenge data.
Some RoBERTa models can learn the law of excluded middle for a single external negation prefix, but they fail to generalize this pattern to semantically similar prefixes (e.g., from 'it is not true that' to 'it is false that').
Inoculation (fine-tuning) on challenge data leads to catastrophic forgetting, altering the models' representations of negation prefixes and reducing their similarity to related prefixes.
Theorem 1 proves that encoder transformers are theoretically capable of modeling the law of excluded middle for arbitrary external negation prefixes, suggesting the practical failure is due to training procedures or data structure, not architectural limitations.
papers.limitation:
Only encoder and encoder-decoder transformers are considered, not decoder-only models like LLaMa-2 or GPT-3.
Challenge data generation uses only MNLI and SNLI datasets, which may contain non-representative data and annotation artifacts.
Only two external negation prefix triggers ('it is not true that' and 'it is false that') are used, limiting the variety of negation studied.
Theorem 1 applies only to encoder transformers and assumes a fixed input length, which may not fully reflect real-world conditions.
future_direction: Evaluation of decoder-only transformer models (e.g., LLaMa-2, GPT-3) on similar negation tasks.
Incorporating a wider variety of negation triggers in challenge data generation.
Exploring training procedures like unlikelihood with reference training or logic-based regularization to improve negation handling.
papers.abstract: NLI tasks necessitate a substantial degree of logical reasoning; as such, the remarkable performance of SoTA transformers on these tasks may lead us to believe that those models have learned to reason logically.The results presented in this paper demonstrate that (i) models fine-tuned on NLI datasets learn to treat external negation as a distractor, effectively ignoring its presence in hypothesis sentences; (ii) several near-SoTA encoder and encoder-decoder transformer models fail to inductively learn the law of the excluded middle for a single external negation prefix with respect to NLI tasks, despite extensive fine-tuning; (iii) those models which are able to learn the law of the excluded middle for a single prefix are unable to generalize this pattern to similar prefixes.Given the critical role of negation in logical reasoning, we may conclude from these findings that transformers do not learn to reason logically when fine-tuned for NLI tasks.Furthermore, these results suggest that transformers may not be able to inductively learn the role of negation with respect to NLI tasks, calling into question their capacity to fully acquire logical reasoning abilities.

papers.title: Controlling the Imprint of Passivization and Negation in Contextualized Representations
papers.research_question: How do passivization and negation affect contextualized word representations, and can removing such information improve word similarity?
papers.core_contribution: Passivization and negation leave a strong imprint on contextualized representations, and neutralizing this information using Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) leads to more similar embeddings for words that should preserve their meaning. Features encoding these transformations are more generalizable in machine translation models than in BERT.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that passivization and negation leave traces in contextualized representations, and that neutralizing this information preserves the similarity of word instances with the same reference. Machine translation embeddings contain more generalizable features for these transformations than BERT embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Passivization and negation leave a strong, classifiable imprint on contextualized word representations.
Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) can effectively remove these traces, reducing classification accuracy to chance level.
Removing the transformation traces improves word similarity, as measured by reduced inter-class distances.
The features encoding the transformations are more generalizable across datasets in machine translation models than in BERT.
The null-space projection does not transfer well across different grammatical categories (e.g., from verbs to nouns).
papers.limitation: The null-space projection learned on one dataset does not transfer well to another dataset for BERT representations, and projections do not transfer well across grammatical categories.
papers.abstract: Contextualized word representations encode rich information about syntax and semantics, alongside specificities of each context of use. While contextual variation does not always reflect actual meaning shifts, it can still reduce the similarity of embeddings for word instances having the same meaning. We explore the imprint of two specific linguistic alternations, namely passivization and negation, on the representations generated by neural models trained with two different objectives: masked language modeling and translation. Our exploration methodology is inspired by an approach previously proposed for removing societal biases from word vectors. We show that passivization and negation leave their traces on the representations, and that neutralizing this information leads to more similar embeddings for words that should preserve their meaning in the transformation. We also find clear differences in how the respective features generalize across datasets.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Neural Natural Language Inference Models Partially Embed Theories of Lexical Entailment and Negation
papers.research_question: Whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a BERT-based model, after fine-tuning, can learn to reason about lexical entailment and negation, and structural evaluations (probes and interventions) provide evidence that the model partially embeds the target monotonicity algorithm.
papers.conclusion: The BERT model at least partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level, in addition to achieving the correct input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets (SNLI/MNLI) fail systematically on examples requiring negation to reverse lexical entailment.
Fine-tuning on a subset of the MoNLI dataset enables models to solve a systematic generalization task requiring lexical entailment and negation.
Probing experiments show that BERT's internal representations correlate with the lexical entailment relation and the algorithm's output.
Interchange intervention experiments show that BERT's causal dynamics mirror the monotonicity algorithm on specific subsets of the MoNLI data.
papers.limitation:
The interchange intervention methodology is not yet formally grounded.
The analysis only shows that BERT mimics the algorithm on subsets of MoNLI, not on the entire dataset.
papers.abstract: We address whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation, using four methods: the behavioral evaluation methods of (1) challenge test sets and (2) systematic generalization tasks, and the structural evaluation methods of (3) probes and (4) interventions. To facilitate this holistic evaluation, we present Monotonicity NLI (MoNLI), a new naturalistic dataset focused on lexical entailment and negation. In our behavioral evaluations, we find that models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets fail systematically on MoNLI examples containing negation, but that MoNLI fine-tuning addresses this failure. In our structural evaluations, we look for evidence that our top-performing BERT-based model has learned to implement the monotonicity algorithm behind MoNLI. Probes yield evidence consistent with this conclusion, and our intervention experiments bolster this, showing that the causal dynamics of the model mirror the causal dynamics of this algorithm on subsets of MoNLI. This suggests that the BERT model at least partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level.

papers.title: Strong hallucinations from negation and how to fix them
papers.research_question: How do language models handle negation and why do they produce strong hallucinations? How can we fix these hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hybrid method (Λ) that treats negation as an operation over latent representations, constraining the evolution of distributions to eliminate strong hallucinations and improve performance on tasks with negation without requiring negative data.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid approach Λ effectively reduces strong hallucinations from negation and improves model performance on logical tasks by constraining the LM's distribution to respect logical semantics.
papers.key_findings:
Language models inevitably produce strong hallucinations due to their distribution over strings not respecting logical properties, as proven theoretically.
The proposed method Λ improves performance on masked knowledge retrieval (MKR) and natural language inference (NLI) tasks with negation.
Λ achieves 0 exact matches on MKR and significant accuracy improvements on NLI (e.g., 13% on one NLI dataset, 91% on another).
Λ uses models fine-tuned only on positive data, avoiding the need for sparse negative data.
Fine-tuned Llama combined with Λ showed a 27% accuracy improvement over Llama alone on ¬SNLI.
papers.limitation:
Tasks with long string output are beyond the paper's scope due to complex evaluations required.
Prompting procedures for Llama were unstable, with slight variations producing quite different results.
papers.abstract: Despite great performance on many tasks, language models (LMs) still struggle with reasoning, sometimes providing responses that cannot possibly be true because they stem from logical incoherence. We call such responses \textit{strong hallucinations} and prove that they follow from an LM's computation of its internal representations for logical operators and outputs from those representations. Focusing on negation, we provide a novel solution in which negation is treated not as another element of a latent representation, but as \textit{an operation over an LM's latent representations that constrains how they may evolve}. We show that our approach improves model performance in cloze prompting and natural language inference tasks with negation without requiring training on sparse negative data.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: LF-Steering: Latent Feature Activation Steering for Enhancing Semantic Consistency in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we precisely identify and modify latent feature representations to improve the semantic consistency of Large Language Models (LLMs) when responding to semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LF-Steering, a novel activation steering method that uses a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to decompose transformer layer hidden states into a sparsely activated, higher-dimensional feature space, enabling precise identification and adjustment of features responsible for semantic inconsistency to improve LLM performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LF-Steering method effectively enhances the semantic consistency of LLMs by enabling precise, feature-level activation steering, leading to significant task performance gains across a range of NLU and NLG datasets.
papers.key_findings:
LF-Steering achieves state-of-the-art performance in enhancing semantic consistency, outperforming baseline activation steering methods on NLU and NLG tasks.
Feature-level steering using SAE features significantly outperforms neuron-level (hidden state) steering, demonstrating the advantage of operating on decoupled feature representations.
The method shows good locality, not negatively impacting performance on out-of-domain datasets and sometimes improving it.
Middle to final transformer layers (layers 17-32 in LLama2-7B-Chat) are most significantly associated with semantic inconsistency.
The effectiveness of the method depends on selecting appropriate hyperparameters, such as the feature difference threshold and steering strength.
papers.limitation: Addressing semantic inconsistency at a single transformer layer may offer only a partial solution, as relevant latent representations may span multiple layers.
future_direction: Focus on identifying and steering circuits across multiple transformer layers to enhance the LLM's semantic consistency.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate inconsistent responses when prompted with semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs. Recently, activation steering, a technique that modulates LLMs' behaviours by adjusting their latent representations during inference time, has been explored to improve the semantic consistency of LLMs. However, these methods typically operate at the model component level, such as layer hidden states or attention head outputs. They face a challenge due to the ``polysemanticity issue'', where the model components of LLMs typically encode multiple entangled features, making precise steering difficult. To address this challenge, we drill down to feature-level representations and propose LF-Steering, a novel activation steering approach to precisely identify latent feature representations responsible for semantic inconsistency. More specifically, our method maps the hidden states of the relevant transformer layer into a sparsely activated, high-dimensional feature space based on a sparse autoencoder (SAE), ensuring model steering based on decoupled feature representations with minimal interference. Comprehensive experiments on NLU and NLG datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in enhancing semantic consistency, resulting in significant performance gains for various NLU and NLG tasks.

papers.title: Do Language Models Understand Anything? On the Ability of LSTMs to Understand Negative Polarity Items
papers.research_question: Does an LSTM language model understand the relationship between negative polarity items and their licensing contexts, and can it detect the scope of the licensing context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that an LSTM language model can detect the relationship between negative polarity items and their licensing contexts, and that the model's hidden representations encode information about the scope of the licensing context.
papers.conclusion: The LSTM model is capable of handling NPI constructions and the licensing signal can be extracted from its hidden representations, paving the way for linking linguistic theory to neural models.
papers.key_findings:
The model assigns lower perplexity to sentences with correct NPI licensing compared to ungrammatical counterparts.
The model shows a strong preference for NPIs in negative contexts over positive contexts.
The model's hidden states can be used to predict the scope of the licensing context with high accuracy.
The model outperforms a baseline using GloVe embeddings in scope detection.
The effect of distance between NPI and licensing context: the model's performance degrades with longer distances.
papers.limitation:
The model's ability to handle NPI constructions degrades with longer distances between the NPI and the licensing context.
The study is limited to a subset of NPIs (those licensed by negative operators) and does not cover the full diversity of NPI constructions.
future_direction: Investigate a wider typological range of NPI constructions
Compare model performance with human judgments
Design entailment tasks based on linguistic hypotheses about NPI licensing
papers.abstract: In this paper, we attempt to link the inner workings of a neural language model to linguistic theory, focusing on a complex phenomenon well discussed in formal linguistics: (negative) polarity items. We briefly discuss the leading hypotheses about the licensing contexts that allow negative polarity items and evaluate to what extent a neural language model has the ability to correctly process a subset of such constructions. We show that the model finds a relation between the licensing context and the negative polarity item and appears to be aware of the scope of this context, which we extract from a parse tree of the sentence. With this research, we hope to pave the way for other studies linking formal linguistics to deep learning.

papers.title: Neural Natural Language Inference Models Partially Embed Theories of\n Lexical Entailment and Negation
papers.research_question: Whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT models, after fine-tuning on MoNLI, can learn to reason about lexical entailment and negation, and structural evaluations indicate they implement an algorithm for monotonicity reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT models can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation, both behaviorally and structurally.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on general NLI datasets fail on MoNLI examples with negation.
Fine-tuning on MoNLI enables models to generalize to new lexical items in negated contexts.
Probes show that BERT representations correlate with lexical entailment relations.
Intervention experiments show that BERT's causal dynamics mirror the monotonicity algorithm on subsets of MoNLI.
BERT at least partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level.
papers.limitation:
The interchange intervention methodology is not yet formally grounded.
The analysis only considered one location for interventions and may not capture all causal dynamics.
papers.abstract:
We address whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can
learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation,
using four methods: the behavioral evaluation methods of (1) challenge test
sets and (2) systematic generalization tasks, and the structural evaluation
methods of (3) probes and (4) interventions. To facilitate this holistic
evaluation, we present Monotonicity NLI (MoNLI), a new naturalistic dataset
focused on lexical entailment and negation. In our behavioral evaluations, we
find that models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets fail systematically on
MoNLI examples containing negation, but that MoNLI fine-tuning addresses this
failure. In our structural evaluations, we look for evidence that our
top-performing BERT-based model has learned to implement the monotonicity
algorithm behind MoNLI. Probes yield evidence consistent with this conclusion,
and our intervention experiments bolster this, showing that the causal dynamics
of the model mirror the causal dynamics of this algorithm on subsets of MoNLI.
This suggests that the BERT model at least partially embeds a theory of lexical
entailment and negation at an algorithmic level.

papers.title: Investigating a neural language model’s replicability of psycholinguistic experiments: A case study of NPI licensing
papers.research_question: Does the neural language model BERT capture syntactic and semantic constraints in Negative Polarity Item (NPI) processing, and does it exhibit processing patterns (including grammatical illusion) similar to humans?
papers.core_contribution: The neural language model BERT is highly sensitive to both syntactic and semantic constraints in NPI processing, and its processing patterns and sensitivities are very close to humans, suggesting its role as a research tool or object in the study of language.
papers.conclusion: BERT exhibits knowledge necessary for processing linguistic input and returns results analogous to human language comprehension, suggesting it can be a testable toolset for linguists and psycholinguists.
papers.key_findings:
BERT successfully discriminates between syntactically correct and incorrect licensor positions for NPIs.
BERT shows susceptibility to grammatical illusion, analogous to human processing errors.
BERT distinguishes between licensors of different semantic strengths (e.g., classic negation 'no' vs. minimal negation 'few').
BERT's evaluation of the licensor 'only' yielded inconsistent results depending on the measurement position (NPI vs. licensor).
Overall, BERT's behavior in NPI processing closely mirrors human psycholinguistic patterns.
papers.limitation:
BERT is bidirectional, which differs from the unidirectional, incremental nature of human sentence processing, making direct comparison of surprisal values problematic.
Inconsistent results for the licensor 'only' depending on the mask position (NPI vs. licensor) indicate complexity in modeling its semantic/pragmatic behavior.
future_direction: Investigate how the transiency and the medium degree of surprisal in BERT's illusion effect are analogous to human processing.
Use BERT for crosslinguistic comparisons, e.g., between retrospective licensing languages (like English) and prospective licensing languages (like Korean).
papers.abstract: The recent success of deep learning neural language models such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) has brought innovations to computational language research. The present study explores the possibility of using a language model in investigating human language processes, based on the case study of negative polarity items (NPIs). We first conducted an experiment with BERT to examine whether the model successfully captures the hierarchical structural relationship between an NPI and its licensor and whether it may lead to an error analogous to the grammatical illusion shown in the psycholinguistic experiment (Experiment 1). We also investigated whether the language model can capture the fine-grained semantic properties of NPI licensors and discriminate their subtle differences on the scale of licensing strengths (Experiment 2). The results of the two experiments suggest that overall, the neural language model is highly sensitive to both syntactic and semantic constraints in NPI processing. The model's processing patterns and sensitivities are shown to be very close to humans, suggesting their role as a research tool or object in the study of language.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Do Language Models Understand Anything? On the Ability of LSTMs to\n Understand Negative Polarity Items
papers.research_question: Do neural language models (specifically LSTMs) understand negative polarity items (NPIs) and their licensing contexts?
papers.core_contribution: The LSTM language model can detect the relationship between negative polarity items and their licensing contexts, and its hidden representations encode information about the scope of the licensing context.
papers.conclusion: The LSTM language model is capable of detecting the relationship between NPIs and their licensing contexts, and the hidden representations contain information about the scope, paving the way for linking linguistic theory to neural models.
papers.key_findings:
The model assigns lower perplexity to sentences with correct NPI licensing compared to ungrammatical counterparts.
The model shows a strong preference for NPIs in negative contexts over positive contexts.
The model's hidden states can be used to predict the scope of the licensing context with high accuracy (89.7%).
The model outperforms a GloVe embedding baseline in scope detection, indicating the LSTM adds significant syntactic information.
The effect of licensing context on NPI processing diminishes as the distance between the NPI and licensor increases.
papers.limitation:
The effect of licensing context on NPI processing diminishes with increased distance between the NPI and licensor.
The study focuses only on a subset of NPIs (those licensed by negative operators), while NPI distribution is highly diverse, requiring more extensive investigation.
Rewriting sentences to create ungrammatical counterparts may result in less probable sentences, potentially confounding perplexity comparisons.
future_direction: Investigate a wider typological range of NPI constructions and how diagnostic tasks translate to other types.
Compare findings to human judgments in syntactic gap-filling tasks.
Devise entailment tasks based on linguistic hypotheses (e.g., downward entailing, non-veridical contexts) to gain deeper semantic insight.
papers.abstract:
In this paper, we attempt to link the inner workings of a neural language
model to linguistic theory, focusing on a complex phenomenon well discussed in
formal linguis- tics: (negative) polarity items. We briefly discuss the leading
hypotheses about the licensing contexts that allow negative polarity items and
evaluate to what extent a neural language model has the ability to correctly
process a subset of such constructions. We show that the model finds a relation
between the licensing context and the negative polarity item and appears to be
aware of the scope of this context, which we extract from a parse tree of the
sentence. With this research, we hope to pave the way for other studies linking
formal linguistics to deep learning.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Don't Think of the White Bear: Ironic Negation in Transformer Models Under Cognitive Load
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do transformer language models show ironic rebound (increased accessibility of a forbidden concept) versus suppression after a negation instruction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit ironic rebound after negation instructions, with semantic distractors causing the strongest rebound and a sparse set of middle-layer attention heads amplifying forbidden tokens while early layers suppress them, linking cognitive predictions to mechanistic insights.
papers.conclusion: LLMs display ironic rebound after a 'do not mention X' instruction, becoming more likely to output X, with circuit tracing showing sparse middle-layer attention heads amplify the forbidden token under load while early layers suppress it.
papers.key_findings:
Ironic rebound occurs in LLMs after negation instructions, with semantic distractors triggering the strongest rebound.
Repetition distractors support suppression, while semantic and syntactic distractors lead to rebound.
Models with sharper polarity separation (between neutral and negative framings) show longer-lasting rebound (higher L50).
Circuit analysis reveals early layers suppress forbidden tokens, while a sparse set of middle-layer attention heads amplify them, causing rebound.
Rebound effect varies across models; GPT-OSS-20B is an outlier showing minimal rebound.
papers.limitation:
Synthetic, templated prompts rather than naturalistic conversational contexts.
Reliance on log-probabilities rather than actual text generation.
Focus on English and single-token target concepts.
Only three distractor types (semantic, syntactic, repetition).
Artificial 'do not mention X' instructions differ from real-world content policies.
future_direction: Mechanistic interpretability work to identify specific circuits responsible for ironic rebound.
Explore more naturalistic settings, including conversational contexts.
Investigate the anomalous behavior of GPT-OSS-20B and mitigation strategies.
papers.abstract: Negation instructions such as 'do not mention $X$' can paradoxically increase the accessibility of $X$ in human thought, a phenomenon known as ironic rebound. Large language models (LLMs) face the same challenge: suppressing a concept requires internally activating it, which may prime rebound instead of avoidance. We investigated this tension with two experiments. \textbf{(1) Load \& content}: after a negation instruction, we vary distractor text (semantic, syntactic, repetition) and measure rebound strength. \textbf{(2) Polarity separation}: We test whether models distinguish neutral from negative framings of the same concept and whether this separation predicts rebound persistence. Results show that rebound consistently arises immediately after negation and intensifies with longer or semantic distractors, while repetition supports suppression. Stronger polarity separation correlates with more persistent rebound. Together, these findings, complemented by a circuit tracing analysis that identifies sparse middle-layer attention heads amplifying forbidden tokens while early layers suppress, link cognitive predictions of ironic rebound with mechanistic insights into long-context interference. To support future work, we release ReboundBench, a dataset of $5,000$ systematically varied negation prompts designed to probe rebound in LLMs.

papers.title: Steering Large Language Models using Conceptors: Improving Addition-Based Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can conceptors be used to improve the precision and effectiveness of activation engineering for steering large language models compared to traditional additive steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces conceptors as a novel steering mechanism for large language models, demonstrating that they provide more precise control and outperform traditional additive steering methods across multiple tasks.
papers.conclusion: Conceptor-based steering outperforms additive methods and offers a more precise and effective way to control LLM outputs, suggesting a shift towards region-based representations in activation engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Conceptor-based steering achieves higher accuracy than additive steering on all function tasks for both GPT-J and GPT-NeoX models.
Mean-centering enhances the performance of both steering methods, but conceptors still outperform even without mean-centering.
Conceptors can be combined using Boolean operations (AND) to steer composite functions, outperforming additive combination of steering vectors.
Steering is most effective in specific layers (9-16 for GPT-J, 10-30 for GPT-NeoX).
The aperture parameter α for conceptors is robust, with α=0.1 performing well across experiments.
papers.limitation:
Conceptors rely on more data points to build accurate representations.
Conceptors are more computationally expensive compared to simple addition-based methods.
Conceptors introduce a new hyperparameter, the aperture α, that may require tuning for optimal performance.
future_direction: Assess the impact of conceptor steering on the model's overall capabilities.
Evaluate performance on more complex behaviors or tasks.
Investigate scalability to larger models.
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed AI, yet reliably controlling their outputs remains a challenge. This paper explores activation engineering, where outputs of pre-trained LLMs are controlled by manipulating their activations at inference time. Unlike traditional methods using a single steering vector, we introduce conceptors - mathematical constructs that represent sets of activation vectors as ellipsoidal regions. Conceptors act as soft projection matrices and offer more precise control over complex activation patterns. Our experiments demonstrate that conceptors outperform traditional methods across multiple steering tasks. We further use Boolean operations on conceptors for combined steering goals that empirically outperform additively combining steering vectors on a set of tasks. These results highlight conceptors as a promising tool for more effective steering of LLMs. Our code is available on github.com/jorispos/conceptorsteering.

papers.title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence
papers.research_question: How is refusal behavior mediated in large language models? Is it controlled by a single direction or by more complex geometric structures such as multiple independent directions and concept cones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a gradient-based representation engineering method (RDO) to identify refusal directions, discovers multi-dimensional refusal cones, and proposes representational independence to characterize independent directions.
papers.conclusion: The work advances understanding of refusal mechanisms in LLMs through gradient-based representation engineering, showing refusal is governed by high-dimensional cones and multiple independent directions, providing a framework for analyzing representational interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based Refusal Direction Optimization (RDO) yields more effective refusal directions with fewer side effects compared to difference-in-means (DIM) baselines.
Refusal behavior is mediated by multi-dimensional polyhedral cones (concept cones) in activation space, not a single linear direction.
Orthogonality does not guarantee independence under intervention; representational independence accounts for linear and non-linear dependencies.
Multiple representationally independent refusal directions exist, indicating distinct underlying mechanisms.
These independent directions can be accessed via input manipulations (e.g., adversarial suffixes) and compositionally ablated to improve jailbreak success.
papers.limitation:
The refusal directions are optimized on the same targets, which may limit their ability to capture fully distinct mechanisms.
Cannot rule out the possibility of other yet-undiscovered regions in the model that mediate refusal.
future_direction: Extending the method to incorporate diverse targets or leveraging reinforcement learning with a judge-based reward function to identify additional independent mechanisms.
Applying the gradient-based representation engineering approach to identify various concepts beyond refusal by changing optimization targets.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) can be circumvented through adversarially crafted inputs, yet the mechanisms by which these attacks bypass safety barriers remain poorly understood. Prior work suggests that a single refusal direction in the model's activation space determines whether an LLM refuses a request. In this study, we propose a novel gradient-based approach to representation engineering and use it to identify refusal directions. Contrary to prior work, we uncover multiple independent directions and even multi-dimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. Moreover, we show that orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention, motivating the notion of representational independence that accounts for both linear and non-linear effects. Using this framework, we identify mechanistically independent refusal directions. We show that refusal mechanisms in LLMs are governed by complex spatial structures and identify functionally independent directions, confirming that multiple distinct mechanisms drive refusal behavior. Our gradient-based approach uncovers these mechanisms and can further serve as a foundation for future work on understanding LLMs.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: A Primer on the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Language Models
papers.core_contribution: Provides a concise technical introduction to interpretability techniques for Transformer-based language models and a comprehensive overview of known internal mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The primer consolidates current interpretability techniques and known mechanisms, providing a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Summarizes known internal mechanisms of Transformer LMs, such as attention patterns and feedforward network functions.
Highlights the residual stream as a key perspective for understanding model computations.
Surveys techniques for behavior localization (e.g., logit attribution, causal interventions) and information decoding (e.g., probing, sparse autoencoders).
papers.abstract: The rapid progress of research aimed at interpreting the inner workings of advanced language models has highlighted a need for contextualizing the insights gained from years of work in this area. This primer provides a concise technical introduction to the current techniques used to interpret the inner workings of Transformer-based language models, focusing on the generative decoder-only architecture. We conclude by presenting a comprehensive overview of the known internal mechanisms implemented by these models, uncovering connections across popular approaches and active research directions in this area.

papers.title: minicons: Enabling Flexible Behavioral and Representational Analyses of Transformer Language Models
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces minicons, an open-source library that provides a standard API for behavioral and representational analyses of transformer language models, facilitating efficient extraction of word/sentence probabilities and contextualized embeddings.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents minicons, a utility tool for analyzing transformer language models, and demonstrates its use in two case studies, showing its potential for facilitating behavioral and representational analyses.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's knowledge of linguistic acceptability emerges at different rates for different phenomena, with some phenomena showing signs of forgetting during training.
On zero-shot abductive reasoning, most models perform near chance, with ALBERT-xxlarge-v2 achieving the best accuracy (0.61) despite being smaller than other models.
Performance on abductive reasoning scales linearly with the logarithm of the number of parameters (R²=0.48), suggesting that scaling alone is unlikely to reach state-of-the-art performance.
future_direction: Integrate newer utility functions into the library and develop detailed tutorials for users.
papers.abstract: We present minicons, an open source library that provides a standard API for researchers interested in conducting behavioral and representational analyses of transformer-based language models (LMs). Specifically, minicons enables researchers to apply analysis methods at two levels: (1) at the prediction level -- by providing functions to efficiently extract word/sentence level probabilities; and (2) at the representational level -- by also facilitating efficient extraction of word/phrase level vectors from one or more layers. In this paper, we describe the library and apply it to two motivating case studies: One focusing on the learning dynamics of the BERT architecture on relative grammatical judgments, and the other on benchmarking 23 different LMs on zero-shot abductive reasoning. minicons is available at https://github.com/kanishkamisra/minicons

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: RepIt: Steering Language Models with Concept-Specific Refusal Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we isolate concept-specific refusal representations in language model activations to enable targeted jailbreaks while preserving refusal on other harmful concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPIT, a framework to isolate concept-specific refusal representations in LM activations, enabling targeted jailbreaks that evade standard safety benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The REPIT framework demonstrates precise concept disentanglement, exposing vulnerabilities in current safety evaluation practices and highlighting the need for more comprehensive, representation-aware assessments.
papers.key_findings:
REPIT can jailbreak target concepts (e.g., weapons of mass destruction) while preserving refusal on non-target harmful concepts, achieving high target attack success rates with minimal spillover.
The edit to the steering vector localizes to just 100-200 neurons, indicating a sparse, high-leverage mechanism.
REPIT is highly data-efficient, producing robust concept vectors from as few as 12 target examples.
Standard safety benchmarks fail to detect models with such targeted, concept-specific jailbreaks, revealing a critical evaluation blind spot.
Disentanglement reveals that target and non-target refusal representations are entangled, and the removed projection can itself induce jailbreaks.
papers.limitation: COSMIC only supports a binary harmful/harmless setup, requiring adaptation for the target/non-target/harmless formulation.
future_direction: Further research using SAE or circuit perspectives to understand the bidirectional effects and heavy-tail neuron phenomena.
Development of more comprehensive, representation-aware safety assessments.
papers.abstract: While activation steering in large language models (LLMs) is a growing area of research, methods can often incur broader effects than desired. This motivates isolation of purer concept vectors to enable targeted interventions and understand LLM behavior at a more granular level. We present RepIt, a simple and data-efficient framework for isolating concept-specific representations. Across five frontier LLMs, RepIt enables precise interventions: it selectively suppresses refusal on targeted concepts while preserving refusal elsewhere, producing models that answer WMD-related questions while still scoring as safe on standard benchmarks. We further show that the corrective signal localizes to just 100-200 neurons and that robust target representations can be extracted from as few as a dozen examples on a single A6000. This efficiency raises a dual concern: manipulations can be performed with modest compute and data to extend to underrepresented data-scarce topics while evading existing benchmarks. By disentangling refusal vectors with RepIt, this work demonstrates that targeted interventions can counteract overgeneralization, laying the foundation for more granular control of model behavior.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
