Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Provably Transformers Harness Multi-Concept Word Semantics for Efficient In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Whether and how do the geometric regularity of the multi-concept-encoded representation facilitate transformer in conducting efficient ICL?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides a fine-grained mathematical analysis to show how transformers leverage the multi-concept semantics of words to enable powerful ICL and excellent out-of-distribution ICL abilities.
papers.conclusion: Transformers harness multi-concept word semantics for efficient in-context learning and out-of-distribution generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Exponential convergence of 0-1 loss for transformers in ICL.
Transformers can achieve Bayes optimal test error with a logarithmic number of iterations.
Multi-concept semantics enable transformers to efficiently perform certain out-of-distribution ICL tasks.
The analysis offers an intuitive explanation for why transformer-based LLMs can leverage polysemous words to tackle diverse, unseen concept-specific tasks.
The findings provide a potential theoretical underpinning for the innovative capabilities of LLMs, including cross-concept knowledge intersection.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) have displayed remarkable creative prowess and emergence capabilities. Existing empirical studies have revealed a strong connection between these LLMs' impressive emergence abilities and their in-context learning (ICL) capacity, allowing them to solve new tasks using only task-specific prompts without further fine-tuning. On the other hand, existing empirical and theoretical studies also show that there is a linear regularity of the multi-concept encoded semantic representation behind transformer-based LLMs. However, existing theoretical work fail to build up an understanding of the connection between this regularity and the innovative power of ICL. Additionally, prior work often focuses on simplified, unrealistic scenarios involving linear transformers or unrealistic loss functions, and they achieve only linear or sub-linear convergence rates. In contrast, this work provides a fine-grained mathematical analysis to show how transformers leverage the multi-concept semantics of words to enable powerful ICL and excellent out-of-distribution ICL abilities, offering insights into how transformers innovate solutions for certain unseen tasks encoded with multiple cross-concept semantics. Inspired by empirical studies on the linear latent geometry of LLMs, the analysis is based on a concept-based low-noise sparse coding prompt model. Leveraging advanced techniques, this work showcases the exponential 0-1 loss convergence over the highly non-convex training dynamics, which pioneeringly incorporates the challenges of softmax self-attention, ReLU-activated MLPs, and cross-entropy loss. Empirical simulations corroborate the theoretical findings.

papers.title: Does Transformer Interpretability Transfer to RNNs?
papers.research_question: Does transformer interpretability transfer to RNNs? Specifically, do contrastive activation addition, the tuned lens, and methods for eliciting latent knowledge work on RNNs like Mamba and RWKV?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that popular transformer interpretability methods (contrastive activation addition, the tuned lens, and methods for eliciting latent knowledge) transfer to state-of-the-art RNN architectures, and that the compressed state of RNNs can be used to enhance activation addition for steering.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability tools designed for transformers largely work out-of-the-box for RNNs, with similar performance, and the compressed state of RNNs can be used to enhance activation addition for steering.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) is effective for steering RNNs, with middle layers showing the greatest effect.
State steering, using the internal state of RNNs, is possible and can be combined with activation steering, though the effects are not additive.
The tuned lens can be applied to RNNs, with perplexity decreasing monotonically with depth, similar to transformers.
Linear probes trained on 'Alice' contexts can predict the correct answer in 'Bob' contexts for RNNs, similar to transformers.
papers.limitation: The work did not explore mechanistic or circuit-based interpretability tools, focusing instead on representation-based methods.
future_direction: Further exploration of the RNN state for extracting latent knowledge or predictions.
Examination of the applicability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to RNNs.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in recurrent neural network architectures, such as Mamba and RWKV, have enabled RNNs to match or exceed the performance of equal-size transformers in terms of language modeling perplexity and downstream evaluations, suggesting that future systems may be built on completely new architectures. In this paper, we examine if selected interpretability methods originally designed for transformer language models will transfer to these up-and-coming recurrent architectures. Specifically, we focus on steering model outputs via contrastive activation addition, on eliciting latent predictions via the tuned lens, and eliciting latent knowledge from models fine-tuned to produce false outputs under certain conditions. Our results show that most of these techniques are effective when applied to RNNs, and we show that it is possible to improve some of them by taking advantage of RNNs' compressed state.

papers.title: Analyzing Encoded Concepts in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether transformer language models encode linguistic concepts in their representations, which concepts dominate the overall structure, and whether the models learn novel concepts beyond linguistic properties.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ConceptX, a framework that uses unsupervised clustering to discover latent concepts in transformer language model representations and aligns them with human-defined concepts to explain how linguistic knowledge is structured across layers and models.
papers.conclusion: ConceptX provides a framework for analyzing encoded concepts in deep NLP models, revealing how linguistic information is structured across layers and highlighting differences between models, with many concepts being compositional or novel.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers of transformer models predominantly capture shallow lexical concepts (e.g., ngrams, suffixes), while middle and higher layers better represent core linguistic concepts (e.g., morphology, syntax, semantics).
Multilingual models (mBERT, XLM-R) show higher alignment with human-defined concepts compared to monolingual models, likely due to more complex training tasks.
Roughly 50% of the encoded concepts discovered align with the suite of human-defined linguistic concepts; the remaining concepts are novel or compositional, involving multiple fine-grained categories.
The extent of alignment varies across different transformer models and different human-defined concepts, influenced by factors like architecture, training data, and objective function.
Models learn multi-faceted concepts that cannot be adequately explained by existing human-defined concepts, indicating the presence of novel semantic relationships.
papers.limitation:
Clustering a large number of high-dimensional vectors is computationally and memory intensive, requiring the use of a subset of data and limiting the number of tokens per word.
The number of clusters (K=1000) was selected empirically rather than through a rigorous optimization method.
papers.abstract: We propose a novel framework ConceptX, to analyze how latent concepts are encoded in representations learned within pre-trained language models. It uses clustering to discover the encoded concepts and explains them by aligning with a large set of human-defined concepts. Our analysis on seven transformer language models reveal interesting insights: i) the latent space within the learned representations overlap with different linguistic concepts to a varying degree, ii) the lower layers in the model are dominated by lexical concepts (e.g., affixation), whereas the core-linguistic concepts (e.g., morphological or syntactic relations) are better represented in the middle and higher layers, iii) some encoded concepts are multi-faceted and cannot be adequately explained using the existing human-defined concepts.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Analyzing the Inner Workings of Transformers in Compositional Generalization
papers.research_question: What type of syntactic features do Transformer models depend on in tasks requiring compositional generalization, and what internal mechanisms do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that Transformer models rely on syntactic features for compositional generalization but also develop non-compositional solutions internally; subnetworks with better generalization performance depend on both syntactic and non-syntactic features.
papers.conclusion: Transformer models develop non-compositional solutions internally and fail to generalize compositionally even when generalization performance is decent, suggesting a need for better inductive bias to utilize syntactic features.
papers.key_findings:
The base Transformer model depends on syntactic features (constituency and dependency) to output correct answers in compositional generalization tasks.
A subnetwork with much better generalization performance than the whole model relies on a non-compositional algorithm in addition to syntactic features.
The subnetwork improves its generalization performance relatively slowly during training compared to its in-distribution performance.
The non-compositional solution is acquired in the early stages of training.
The model's reliance on syntactic features varies between machine translation and semantic parsing tasks.
papers.limitation:
The compositional generalization tasks are based on synthetically generated datasets and might not represent the variety in natural language expressions.
The results may not transfer to larger models because the experiments used relatively small models trained on a small synthetic dataset.
future_direction: Consider other generalization patterns or other linguistic features to obtain a more profound insight into the linguistic competence of neural models.
papers.abstract: The compositional generalization abilities of neural models have been sought after for human-like linguistic competence. The popular method to evaluate such abilities is to assess the models' input-output behavior. However, that does not reveal the internal mechanisms, and the underlying competence of such models in compositional generalization remains unclear. To address this problem, we explore the inner workings of a Transformer model by finding an existing subnetwork that contributes to the generalization performance and by performing causal analyses on how the model utilizes syntactic features. We find that the model depends on syntactic features to output the correct answer, but that the subnetwork with much better generalization performance than the whole model relies on a non-compositional algorithm in addition to the syntactic features. We also show that the subnetwork improves its generalization performance relatively slowly during the training compared to the in-distribution one, and the non-compositional solution is acquired in the early stages of the training.

papers.title: The Stem Cell Hypothesis: Dilemma behind Multi-Task Learning with Transformer Encoders
papers.research_question: Why does multi-task learning (MTL) with transformer encoders on distinct core NLP tasks lead to worse performance than single-task learning, and is there a subset of attention heads that are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for all?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Stem Cell Hypothesis, which states that a subset of attention heads (stem cells) are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks, leading to interference and worse performance in multi-task learning.
papers.conclusion: The Stem Cell Hypothesis sheds light on the dilemma of multi-task learning with transformer encoders, indicating that attention heads cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks without interference, and suggests a direction for future MTL research by wisely assigning heads to tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-task learning on five core NLP tasks (POS, NER, DEP, CON, SRL) results in lower performance than single-task learning for all tasks.
Pruning analysis reveals that all five tasks rely on a similar set of attention heads, primarily in middle layers (5-8), which are termed 'stem cells'.
Even without fine-tuning, certain attention heads (stem cells) show high probing accuracy for specific linguistic labels, demonstrating their pluripotency.
During single-task learning, stem cells become specialized for the task, but during multi-task learning, they lose specialization due to conflicting training signals.
The Stem Cell Hypothesis is validated by novel parameter-free probes that show how attention heads are transformed during training, with MTL often degrading probing and task performance.
future_direction: Adapt the work to more tasks and languages for broader generality.
Design another probing method for deeper analysis in constituency parsing (CON).
papers.abstract: Multi-task learning with transformer encoders (MTL) has emerged as a powerful technique to improve performance on closely-related tasks for both accuracy and efficiency while a question still remains whether or not it would perform as well on tasks that are distinct in nature. We first present MTL results on five NLP tasks, POS, NER, DEP, CON, and SRL, and depict its deficiency over single-task learning. We then conduct an extensive pruning analysis to show that a certain set of attention heads get claimed by most tasks during MTL, who interfere with one another to fine-tune those heads for their own objectives. Based on this finding, we propose the Stem Cell Hypothesis to reveal the existence of attention heads naturally talented for many tasks that cannot be jointly trained to create adequate embeddings for all of those tasks. Finally, we design novel parameter-free probes to justify our hypothesis and demonstrate how attention heads are transformed across the five tasks during MTL through label analysis. papers.title: InverseScope: Scalable Activation Inversion for Interpreting Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to interpret neural activations in large language models via input inversion with minimal assumptions, and scale this approach to larger models and practical tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InverseScope, a scalable activation inversion framework for interpreting LLMs with minimal assumptions, enabling systematic and quantitative analysis of internal representations.
papers.conclusion: InverseScope scales inversion-based interpretability to larger LLMs, providing a rigorous framework for analyzing feature representations and offering new mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
InverseScope significantly improves sampling efficiency over prior inversion methods, reducing refusal rates.
In the IOI task, it identifies attention heads that encode object and subject features, aligning with known circuits.
It outperforms sparse autoencoders in attribute identification on the RAVEL dataset.
In ICL tasks, it explains the emergence of task vectors by showing the separation of task and query features in attention layers.
papers.limitation:
Does not scale to long input sequences.
Hypothesis generation still requires human involvement.
future_direction: Scaling to long input sequences
Automating hypothesis generation
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) is a central challenge in interpretability research. Existing feature interpretability methods often rely on strong assumptions about the structure of representations that may not hold in practice. In this work, we introduce InverseScope, an assumption-light and scalable framework for interpreting neural activations via input inversion. Given a target activation, we define a distribution over inputs that generate similar activations and analyze this distribution to infer the encoded information. To address the inefficiency of sampling in high-dimensional spaces, we propose a novel conditional generation architecture that significantly improves sample efficiency compared to previous method. We further introduce a quantitative evaluation protocol that tests interpretability hypotheses using the feature consistency rate computed over the sampled inputs. InverseScope scales inversion-based interpretability methods to larger models and practical tasks, enabling systematic and quantitative analysis of internal representations in real-world LLMs.

papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: The Lazy Neuron Phenomenon: On Emergence of Activation Sparsity in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the prevalence, causes, and benefits of activation sparsity in Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that activation sparsity is a prevalent phenomenon in Transformers, arising from training dynamics, and that enforcing sparsity via Top-k Transformers improves efficiency, robustness, and calibration.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation sparsity is a fundamental property of trained Transformers with benefits for efficiency and reliability, and it may stem from training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Activation sparsity is prevalent in Transformers for both NLP and vision tasks, across all layers.
Larger Transformers (deeper and wider) are sparser in terms of percentage of nonzero activations.
Sparsity emerges even with random labels, random images, or infinite data, suggesting it is due to training dynamics rather than dataset properties.
Sparsity reduces FLOPs and can improve computational efficiency during inference.
Enforcing sparser activation via Top-k Transformers improves robustness to noisy training data, input corruptions, and calibration of prediction confidence.
papers.limitation: The benefit of sparse activation is not fully realized due to lack of hardware support for sparse computation.
papers.abstract: This paper studies the curious phenomenon for machine learning models with Transformer architectures that their activation maps are sparse. By activation map we refer to the intermediate output of the multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) after a ReLU activation function, and by sparse we mean that on average very few entries (e.g., 3.0% for T5-Base and 6.3% for ViT-B16) are nonzero for each input to MLP. Moreover, larger Transformers with more layers and wider MLP hidden dimensions are sparser as measured by the percentage of nonzero entries. Through extensive experiments we demonstrate that the emergence of sparsity is a prevalent phenomenon that occurs for both natural language processing and vision tasks, on both training and evaluation data, for Transformers of various configurations, at layers of all depth levels, as well as for other architectures including MLP-mixers and 2-layer MLPs. We show that sparsity also emerges using training datasets with random labels, or with random inputs, or with infinite amount of data, demonstrating that sparsity is not a result of a specific family of datasets. We discuss how sparsity immediately implies a way to significantly reduce the FLOP count and improve efficiency for Transformers. Moreover, we demonstrate perhaps surprisingly that enforcing an even sparser activation via Top-k thresholding with a small value of k brings a collection of desired but missing properties for Transformers, namely less sensitivity to noisy training data, more robustness to input corruptions, and better calibration for their prediction confidence.

papers.title: Word Meanings in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How are word meanings represented in transformer language models? Specifically, do transformer models use a lexical store that encodes semantic information in static token embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: The static token embeddings in transformer language models encode a wide variety of semantic information, supporting the idea that LLMs use a lexical store for word meanings and ruling out meaning eliminativist hypotheses.
papers.conclusion: Static embeddings in transformer models store meaningful semantic information, not just syntactic and surface-level features, indicating LLMs require a lexical store of semantic information for understanding text.
papers.key_findings:
Manual inspection of k-means clusters from RoBERTa-base static embeddings reveals many clusters organized by semantic categories (e.g., colors, tools, medical terms).
Quantitative analysis shows clusters are sensitive to psycholinguistic attributes (valence, concreteness, iconicity, taboo, age of acquisition), indicating semantic information is encoded.
The findings rule out meaning eliminativist hypotheses that static embeddings contain little semantic information.
The static embedding space encodes both taxonomic and thematic relations among words.
Some clusters capture worldly information (e.g., political names, sports teams) in addition to semantic features.
papers.limitation:
The iconicity findings are limited, with only 9 sensitive clusters and no clear iconicity-related features upon manual inspection; iconicity may correlate with surface features like syllable count.
The taboo attribute list is small (1,085 tokens), leading to sampling errors and a small number of sensitive clusters.
Clusters sensitive to an attribute might be sensitive to correlative properties rather than the attribute itself.
future_direction: Using alternative embeddings and clustering algorithms (e.g., variations of the EM algorithm).
Using alternative null hypotheses in statistical tests.
Considering subsets of corpora partitioned by source classifications (e.g., cultural biases, sub-populations, settings) to test for idiosyncratic meanings.
papers.abstract: We investigate how word meanings are represented in the transformer language models. Specifically, we focus on whether transformer models employ something analogous to a lexical store - where each word has an entry that contains semantic information. To do this, we extracted the token embedding space of RoBERTa-base and k-means clustered it into 200 clusters. In our first study, we then manually inspected the resultant clusters to consider whether they are sensitive to semantic information. In our second study, we tested whether the clusters are sensitive to five psycholinguistic measures: valence, concreteness, iconicity, taboo, and age of acquisition. Overall, our findings were very positive - there is a wide variety of semantic information encoded within the token embedding space. This serves to rule out certain "meaning eliminativist" hypotheses about how transformer LLMs process semantic information.

papers.title: Transformers as Multi-task Learners: Decoupling Features in Hidden Markov Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformers achieve multi-task generalization? Specifically, what are the layerwise mechanisms by which they represent and process sequential information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers learn local features in lower layers and decoupled, temporally disentangled features in upper layers when modeling Hidden Markov Models, and provides theoretical constructions that align with these observations.
papers.conclusion: This work advances theoretical and empirical understanding of how Transformers achieve strong generalization across sequence learning tasks, showing they transition from local feature learning in lower layers to decoupled representations in upper layers, providing a principled explanation for their expressiveness and efficiency in multi-task and in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Well-trained Transformers achieve high accuracy under in-context learning on HMMs, with performance improving as more input-output examples are provided or as sequence length increases.
Lower layers of Transformers focus on learning local representations, primarily influenced by neighboring tokens.
Upper layers develop decoupled, temporally disentangled representations that are less tied to specific input positions and encode higher-level abstractions.
Transformers gradually recognize task identity across layers, with hidden state identification occurring earlier than task identification, indicating a layerwise processing hierarchy.
The theoretical construction demonstrates that Transformers can approximate low-rank HMMs using a fixed-length memory structure, enabling effective in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Analysis is limited to Hidden Markov Models and may not generalize to more complex settings.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more general assumptions and more complex model settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer based models have shown remarkable capabilities in sequence learning across a wide range of tasks, often performing well on specific task by leveraging input-output examples. Despite their empirical success, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains limited. In this work, we investigate the layerwise behavior of Transformers to uncover the mechanisms underlying their multi-task generalization ability. Taking explorations on a typical sequence model, i.e, Hidden Markov Models, which are fundamental to many language tasks, we observe that: first, lower layers of Transformers focus on extracting feature representations, primarily influenced by neighboring tokens; second, on the upper layers, features become decoupled, exhibiting a high degree of time disentanglement. Building on these empirical insights, we provide theoretical analysis for the expressiveness power of Transformers. Our explicit constructions align closely with empirical observations, providing theoretical support for the Transformer's effectiveness and efficiency on sequence learning across diverse tasks.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: Codebook Features: Sparse and Discrete Interpretability for Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can we train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into codebook features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces codebook features, a method to make neural network hidden states sparse and discrete via vector quantization bottlenecks, enabling improved interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: Codebook features are a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks, providing a sparse, discrete interface for understanding and steering model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can operate with extreme sparse, discrete bottlenecks at each layer with only modest performance degradation.
In a finite state machine task, codebooks overcome superposition by assigning distinct states to discrete codes, and activating a state's code causes the network to behave as if in that state.
In language models, codebooks learn codes representing diverse, disentangled concepts (e.g., topics, emotions, syntax).
Activating topic-related codes during inference can steer language model generations towards those topics.
Codes are better classifiers of simple textual features than individual neurons in the network.
papers.limitation:
Codebook models exhibit modest degradation in performance compared to the original models.
In larger models, many codes do not have a comprehensible interpretation.
future_direction: Understanding circuits and weights by leveraging the sparse, discrete nature of codebooks.
Understanding adversarial examples by identifying which codes shift to cause misclassifications.
Improving interpretability in larger models by using larger codebooks or analyzing code co-occurrence.
Understanding shared representations across domains and modalities (e.g., text and image).
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging in part because of the dense, continuous nature of their hidden states. We explore whether we can train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into what we call codebook features. Codebook features are produced by finetuning neural networks with vector quantization bottlenecks at each layer, producing a network whose hidden features are the sum of a small number of discrete vector codes chosen from a larger codebook. Surprisingly, we find that neural networks can operate under this extreme bottleneck with only modest degradation in performance. This sparse, discrete bottleneck also provides an intuitive way of controlling neural network behavior: first, find codes that activate when the desired behavior is present, then activate those same codes during generation to elicit that behavior. We validate our approach by training codebook Transformers on several different datasets. First, we explore a finite state machine dataset with far more hidden states than neurons. In this setting, our approach overcomes the superposition problem by assigning states to distinct codes, and we find that we can make the neural network behave as if it is in a different state by activating the code for that state. Second, we train Transformer language models with up to 410M parameters on two natural language datasets. We identify codes in these models representing diverse, disentangled concepts (ranging from negative emotions to months of the year) and find that we can guide the model to generate different topics by activating the appropriate codes during inference. Overall, codebook features appear to be a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks and interpretability. Our codebase and models are open-sourced at https://github.com/taufeeque9/codebook-features.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Bigram Subnetworks: Mapping to Next Tokens in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer language models make bigram predictions, and can we identify minimal subnetworks that are both necessary and sufficient for these predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Bigram subnetworks—minimal subsets of parameters concentrated in the first MLP layer—are both necessary and sufficient for basic next token predictions in Transformer language models and drive the transformation from current to next token activations.
papers.conclusion: Bigram subnetworks are minimal, interpretable, and critical for language model performance, and they can serve as a foundation for building up more complex circuits in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Bigram subnetworks exist in models up to 1B parameters, consist of ~10M parameters regardless of model size, and achieve bigram surprisal correlations >0.95.
Bigram subnetworks are concentrated in the first Transformer MLP layer throughout pretraining.
Bigram subnetworks recreate the first-layer transformation that aligns activations with next token predictions rather than current token representations.
Ablating bigram subnetworks drastically hurts language modeling performance, demonstrating their necessity.
Bigram subnetworks overlap significantly with subnetworks trained for optimal pruning.
papers.limitation: The paper does not definitively show that language models make intermediate bigram predictions; the tuned lens used to probe intermediate predictions may be too strong and yield false positives.
future_direction: Using bigram subnetworks as a foundation to build up and study more complex circuits.
Determining where intermediate next token predictions are encoded in language model activations.
papers.abstract: In Transformer language models, activation vectors transform from current token embeddings to next token predictions as they pass through the model. To isolate a minimal form of this transformation, we identify language model subnetworks that make bigram predictions, naive next token predictions based only on the current token. We find that bigram subnetworks can be found in fully trained language models up to 1B parameters, and these subnetworks are critical for model performance even when they consist of less than 0.2% of model parameters. Bigram subnetworks are concentrated in the first Transformer MLP layer, and they overlap significantly with subnetworks trained to optimally prune a given model. Mechanistically, the bigram subnetworks often recreate a pattern from the full models where the first layer induces a sharp change that aligns activations with next token predictions rather than current token representations. Our results demonstrate that bigram subnetworks comprise a minimal subset of parameters that are both necessary and sufficient for basic next token predictions in language models, and they help drive the transformation from current to next token activations in the residual stream. These subnetworks can lay a foundation for studying more complex language model circuits by building up from a minimal circuit.

papers.title: The Knowledge Microscope: Features as Better Analytical Lenses than Neurons
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether features (obtained via Sparse Autoencoders) are better analytical units than neurons for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in language models, addressing challenges of limited knowledge expression, poor interpretability, polysemanticity, and performance in downstream tasks like privacy erasure.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that features extracted via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are superior analytical units to neurons for studying factual knowledge in language models, exhibiting stronger impact on knowledge expression, better interpretability, stronger monosemanticity, and enabling more effective privacy erasure through the proposed FeatureEdit method.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that features are better analytical units than neurons for understanding factual knowledge in language models, and the proposed FeatureEdit method effectively leverages features for privacy erasure.
papers.key_findings:
SAE is effective in decomposing neurons into features for studying factual knowledge mechanisms.
Features, especially post-MLP features, have a stronger impact on knowledge expression than neurons.
Features demonstrate superior interpretability compared to neurons.
Features exhibit stronger monosemanticity, with clear activation patterns for related facts and inactivity for unrelated ones.
The proposed feature-based editing method, FeatureEdit, outperforms neuron-based methods in erasing privacy-sensitive knowledge while maintaining better generalization and causing less damage to general model capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The mapping from features back to weights is indirect and sub-optimal, requiring reconstruction.
The clustering phenomenon of SAE features and their stability across different numbers of features require further investigation.
future_direction: Investigate the inherent stable structure of SAE feature space and whether it is truly insensitive to the number of features.
Improve the mapping from features back to weights for more direct model editing.
papers.abstract: Previous studies primarily utilize MLP neurons as units of analysis for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in Language Models (LMs); however, neurons suffer from polysemanticity, leading to limited knowledge expression and poor interpretability. In this paper, we first conduct preliminary experiments to validate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) can effectively decompose neurons into features, which serve as alternative analytical units. With this established, our core findings reveal three key advantages of features over neurons: (1) Features exhibit stronger influence on knowledge expression and superior interpretability. (2) Features demonstrate enhanced monosemanticity, showing distinct activation patterns between related and unrelated facts. (3) Features achieve better privacy protection than neurons, demonstrated through our proposed FeatureEdit method, which significantly outperforms existing neuron-based approaches in erasing privacy-sensitive information from LMs.Code and dataset will be available.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders be used to decompose and interpret steering vectors?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why directly applying sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two main reasons why sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide misleading decompositions of steering vectors: (1) steering vectors are out-of-distribution for SAEs, and (2) SAEs cannot represent negative coefficients which are meaningful in steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors is misleading due to out-of-distribution and non-negativity constraints; alternative approaches such as learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors have significantly smaller L2-norms than model activations, causing the SAE encoder bias to dominate the decomposition and yield misleading results.
Scaling steering vectors does not resolve the out-of-distribution issue because steering vectors lack default components present in model activations.
SAEs restrict decompositions to non-negative coefficients, but steering vectors have meaningful negative projections in feature directions.
Negative projections in steering vectors can cause spurious positive activations in SAE features due to negative cosine similarities between features.
These issues explain prior observations of irrelevant features in SAE decompositions and the failure of SAE-reconstructed vectors to retain steering properties.
papers.limitation:
The proposed alternative method of learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis requires two SAE decompositions per difference vector, increasing the potential impact of SAE error.
The corrigibility steering vectors may include confounding features related to computer science and language modeling.
future_direction: Explore learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis and establish evaluation metrics to compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a promising approach to control the behaviour of large language models. However, their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) may offer a potential method to interpret steering vectors, recent findings show that SAE-reconstructed vectors often lack the steering properties of the original vectors. This paper investigates why directly applying SAEs to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions, identifying two reasons: (1) steering vectors fall outside the input distribution for which SAEs are designed, and (2) steering vectors can have meaningful negative projections in feature directions, which SAEs are not designed to accommodate. These limitations hinder the direct use of SAEs for interpreting steering vectors.

papers.title: Extending Activation Steering to Broad Skills and Multiple Behaviours
papers.research_question: Can we extend activation steering to broad skills and multiple behaviours?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can be applied to broad skills (coding) with similar effectiveness as narrow skills, and simultaneous injection of multiple steering vectors at different layers is more promising than combining them into a single vector.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering can be extended to broad skills and multiple behaviours, with simultaneous steering being a promising direction.
papers.key_findings:
Steering to reduce general coding ability is competitive with steering to reduce Python-specific ability.
Individual steering vectors for behaviours like myopia and wealth-seeking are effective.
Combining multiple steering vectors into one vector is largely unsuccessful.
Simultaneous injection of individual steering vectors at different layers is promising and has minor alignment tax.
Steering at layer 0 for coding ability had an opposite effect, possibly due to copy suppression.
papers.limitation:
The flexibility of activation steering makes finding optimal setups non-trivial.
It is unclear whether reductions in matching scores (e.g., a 20% reduction in coding accuracy) translate to real-world risk reduction.
future_direction: Testing with other models to understand the general working of activation steering.
Using different injection coefficients for different steering vectors in simultaneous steering.
Generating and injecting steering vectors at different places within a layer (e.g., attention and MLP components).
Steering against alternative programming languages to further investigate broad steering.
papers.abstract: Current large language models have dangerous capabilities, which are likely to become more problematic in the future. Activation steering techniques can be used to reduce risks from these capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the efficacy of activation steering for broad skills and multiple behaviours. First, by comparing the effects of reducing performance on general coding ability and Python-specific ability, we find that steering broader skills is competitive to steering narrower skills. Second, we steer models to become more or less myopic and wealth-seeking, among other behaviours. In our experiments, combining steering vectors for multiple different behaviours into one steering vector is largely unsuccessful. On the other hand, injecting individual steering vectors at different places in a model simultaneously is promising.

papers.title: Representation Surgery: Theory and Practice of Affine Steering
papers.research_question: How can we optimally steer language model representations using affine transformations to reduce undesirable behaviors like bias and toxicity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper derives two optimal affine steering functions (mean matching and mean+covariance matching) under guardedness constraints, providing theoretical justification for existing steering approaches and introducing an improved method for bias and toxicity mitigation.
papers.conclusion: Affine steering functions, particularly mean and covariance matching, are effective for mitigating bias and toxicity in language models, offering a theoretically grounded and practical approach for representation surgery.
papers.key_findings:
Mean and covariance matching steering (MiMiC) reduces bias more effectively than mean matching alone, as shown by lower TPR gap and reduced bias by neighbors.
Affine steering functions can mitigate toxicity in text generation without fine-tuning, though they do not reach state-of-the-art performance compared to methods that require gradient computation or fine-tuning.
The derived steering functions provably remove bias by neighbors in expectation when matching both means and covariances.
Steering representations towards a target concept (e.g., non-toxic) is more suitable for toxicity mitigation than concept erasure, which might erase the model's ability to distinguish between concepts.
The methods are effective across different models (BERT, GPT-2, Llama2) and tasks (classification, generation).
papers.limitation:
The linear nature of the affine transformations may limit their effectiveness compared to non-linear methods.
There is a disparity between the training distribution (last token representations) and inference-time usage (applying the intervention at each generation step) for toxicity mitigation, which may affect performance.
papers.abstract: Language models often exhibit undesirable behavior, e.g., generating toxic or gender-biased text. In the case of neural language models, an encoding of the undesirable behavior is often present in the model's representations. Thus, one natural (and common) approach to prevent the model from exhibiting undesirable behavior is to steer the model's representations in a manner that reduces the probability of it generating undesirable text. This paper investigates the formal and empirical properties of steering functions, i.e., transformation of the neural language model's representations that alter its behavior. First, we derive two optimal, in the least-squares sense, affine steering functions under different constraints. Our theory provides justification for existing approaches and offers a novel, improved steering approach. Second, we offer a series of experiments that demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of the methods in mitigating bias and reducing toxic generation.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: How to Plant Trees in Language Models: Data and Architectural Effects on the Emergence of Syntactic Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: What architectural features and pre-training data properties contribute to the emergence of hierarchical syntactic inductive biases in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that model depth is more critical than width for hierarchical syntactic generalization in Transformers, and that pre-training on simpler language like child-directed speech induces such biases with orders-of-magnitude less data than web text.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that model depth is more important than other architectural components for hierarchical generalization, and that simpler pre-training data leads to faster acquisition of syntactic inductive biases, suggesting Transformers may be more data-efficient in cognitively plausible settings.
papers.key_findings:
Model depth has a greater impact on hierarchical generalization than model width or number of parameters alone.
Pre-training on child-directed speech enables hierarchical generalization with far less data (5M words) compared to Wikipedia or web text (100M-1B words).
The number of parameters does not monotonically predict syntactic generalization accuracy.
Syntactic generalization accuracy correlates with language modeling performance and downstream task performance.
Simpler language, such as Simple Wikipedia, also induces hierarchical biases more efficiently than standard Wikipedia.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to other types of encoder-decoder models, encoder-only, or decoder-only models.
Analysis is based only on English and two syntactic transformations, which may not cover all linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Using methods to measure the tree-likeness of Transformer representations during pre-training.
Disentangling the effects of lexical and syntactic complexity in pre-training data.
Exploring a two-phase 'starting small' pre-training approach.
papers.abstract: Accurate syntactic representations are essential for robust generalization in natural language. Recent work has found that pre-training can teach language models to rely on hierarchical syntactic features - as opposed to incorrect linear features - when performing tasks after fine-tuning. We test what aspects of pre-training are important for endowing encoder-decoder Transformers with an inductive bias that favors hierarchical syntactic generalizations. We focus on architectural features (depth, width, and number of parameters), as well as the genre and size of the pre-training corpus, diagnosing inductive biases using two syntactic transformation tasks: question formation and passivization, both in English. We find that the number of parameters alone does not explain hierarchical generalization: model depth plays greater role than model width. We also find that pre-training on simpler language, such as child-directed speech, induces a hierarchical bias using an order-of-magnitude less data than pre-training on more typical datasets based on web text or Wikipedia; this suggests that in cognitively plausible language acquisition settings, neural language models may be more data-efficient than previously thought.

papers.title: Analyze Feature Flow to Enhance Interpretation and Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do features discovered by sparse autoencoders evolve across consecutive layers of large language models, and how can this understanding be used for interpretability and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a data-free cosine similarity method to map Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across transformer layers, creating flow graphs that reveal feature evolution and enable precise model steering through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-layer feature mapping framework provides granular interpretability of feature evolution in LLMs and offers a new, transparent method for steering model behavior through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Cosine similarity between SAE decoder weights effectively identifies feature relationships across layers, validated against activation correlations.
Feature formation follows distinct patterns: early layers show high entropy and feature birth, middle layers stabilize, and later layers primarily propagate existing features.
Deactivating predecessor features identified by the top-1 cosine match is causally effective, outperforming random selection.
Multi-layer steering using flow graphs is more effective and less sensitive to hyperparameters than single-layer interventions.
Flow graphs provide mechanistic insights, revealing how semantic meaning (e.g., 'particle physics') evolves and transforms across the model's computational pathway.
papers.limitation: The current steering procedure operates locally on hidden states and may not fully redirect the model's computational trajectory to a different 'minima' for truly efficient deactivation or activation.
future_direction: Further research on flow graphs as a unit of study for model interpretability.
Extending the steering experiments and flow graph analysis to other model architectures like Llama Scope.
Investigating the method's applicability and performance across a wider range of models and SAE training configurations.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new approach to systematically map features discovered by sparse autoencoder across consecutive layers of large language models, extending earlier work that examined inter-layer feature links. By using a data-free cosine similarity technique, we trace how specific features persist, transform, or first appear at each stage. This method yields granular flow graphs of feature evolution, enabling fine-grained interpretability and mechanistic insights into model computations. Crucially, we demonstrate how these cross-layer feature maps facilitate direct steering of model behavior by amplifying or suppressing chosen features, achieving targeted thematic control in text generation. Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: Temporal Alignment of Time Sensitive Facts with Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: Can activation engineering be used to temporally align LLMs to improve factual recall without training or dataset creation?
papers.core_contribution: Activation engineering can temporally align LLMs to improve factual recall without training, achieving performance comparable to fine-tuning but with greater computational efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Activation engineering provides a computationally efficient alternative to fine-tuning for temporal alignment of LLMs, achieving similar improvements in factual recall.
papers.key_findings:
Activation engineering improves factual recall for time-sensitive questions, with up to 44% and 16% improvement over relative and explicit prompting respectively.
Multi-layer activation engineering with contrasting prompts is effective, especially in lower layers of the transformer.
Activation engineering is computationally more efficient than fine-tuning, requiring only inference-capable GPUs and minimal time.
The method achieves similar results to fine-tuning without needing pre-aligned datasets.
Activation engineering works best when applied to lower layers (4-14 for 7b/13b, 9-24 for 70b), with higher layers showing reduced influence.
papers.limitation:
AE applied to isolated LLMs with no access to external information, and not investigated with RAG or knowledge editing.
Knowledge cutoff date of September 2022 limits experiments.
Fine-tuning hyperparameters were not optimized and limited GPU resources led to suboptimal fine-tuning for LLaMA2-70b.
future_direction: Using AE temporal alignment in conjunction with knowledge hypernetwork methodologies for updated knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on diverse and often conflicting knowledge spanning multiple domains and time periods. Some of this knowledge is only valid within specific temporal contexts, such as answering the question, "Who is the President of the United States in 2022?" Ensuring LLMs generate time appropriate responses is crucial for maintaining relevance and accuracy. In this work we explore activation engineering as a method for temporally aligning LLMs to improve factual recall without any training or dataset creation. In this research we explore an activation engineering technique to ground three versions of LLaMA 2 to specific points in time and examine the effects of varying injection layers and prompting strategies. Our experiments demonstrate up to a 44% and 16% improvement in relative and explicit prompting respectively, achieving comparable performance to the fine-tuning method proposed by Zhao et al. (2024) . Notably, our approach achieves similar results to the fine-tuning baseline while being significantly more computationally efficient and requiring no pre-aligned datasets.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: Introduction to Transformers: an NLP Perspective
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive introduction to the Transformer architecture, covering its basic components, variants, and applications in natural language processing and beyond.
papers.conclusion: The paper offers a comprehensive overview of Transformers, highlighting their architecture, improvements, and applications, and notes the ongoing evolution of these models.
papers.key_findings:
The Transformer architecture, based on self-attention and feed-forward networks, has become the dominant model in NLP.
Various improvements have been made to the Transformer for efficiency (e.g., sparse attention, linear attention) and accuracy (e.g., deep and wide models).
Transformers have been successfully applied to a wide range of tasks beyond NLP, including computer vision and multimodal processing.
The paper discusses the evolution of Transformers, including syntax-aware models and efficient architectures.
The paper highlights the flexibility of Transformers and their ability to handle long-range dependencies.
papers.limitation: The paper cannot cover all model details or all technical areas due to the rapid evolution of the field.
papers.abstract: Transformers have dominated empirical machine learning models of natural language processing. In this paper, we introduce basic concepts of Transformers and present key techniques that form the recent advances of these models. This includes a description of the standard Transformer architecture, a series of model refinements, and common applications. Given that Transformers and related deep learning techniques might be evolving in ways we have never seen, we cannot dive into all the model details or cover all the technical areas. Instead, we focus on just those concepts that are helpful for gaining a good understanding of Transformers and their variants. We also summarize the key ideas that impact this field, thereby yielding some insights into the strengths and limitations of these models.

papers.title: There Is More to Refusal in Large Language Models than a Single Direction
papers.research_question: How different are the refusal directions when computed for different types of refusal behavior beyond safety, and how do these directions get expressed in the latent space such that they facilitate various styles of refusal under a similar intervention mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal behavior in LLMs is mediated by multiple geometrically distinct activation-space directions, but linear steering along any refusal-related direction acts as a one-dimensional control knob for refusal, with differences primarily in refusal style. Sparse autoencoders reveal a structured internal representation with a shared core of refusal latents and a long tail of style-specific latents.
papers.conclusion: The internal structure of refusal is rich and structured, but linear control flattens this complexity, highlighting the limits of linear interpretability for aligned model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Different refusal categories correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space.
