papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: T3-Vis: visual analytic for Training and fine-Tuning Transformers in NLP
papers.research_question: How can we design a visual analytic framework to assist researchers in understanding and interpreting the training and fine-tuning processes of Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents T3-Vis, a visual analytic framework that integrates multiple interactive visualizations to help researchers understand and interpret the training and fine-tuning of Transformer models by providing insights into hidden states, attention patterns, and training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: T3-Vis is an effective framework for interpreting Transformer models during training and fine-tuning, and it helps identify potential directions to improve task performance.
papers.key_findings:
In extractive summarization, important attention heads exhibit patterns where tokens attend to other tokens of the same word, tokens within the same sentence, and adjacent tokens.
In topic classification, the framework helped identify misclassified examples and revealed that the model sometimes focuses on unimportant details or fails when background knowledge is required.
The framework was found useful by researchers in a focus group for interpreting model behavior and identifying potential improvements.
papers.limitation:
The interface is more useful for classification problems with well-defined evaluation metrics.
There is information loss intrinsic in the dimension reduction methods used for visualization.
The front-end needs optimization to support visualization of large-scale datasets.
future_direction: Extend the framework to provide more advanced visualization for custom Transformers, such as models with more complex connections (e.g., parallel attention layers) or advanced attention mechanisms (e.g., sparse attention).
papers.abstract: Transformers are the dominant architecture in NLP, but their training and fine-tuning is still very challenging. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of a visual analytic framework for assisting researchers in such process, by providing them with valuable insights about the model's intrinsic properties and behaviours. Our framework offers an intuitive overview that allows the user to explore different facets of the model (e.g., hidden states, attention) through interactive visualization, and allows a suite of built-in algorithms that compute the importance of model components and different parts of the input sequence. Case studies and feedback from a user focus group indicate that the framework is useful, and suggest several improvements. Our framework is available at:

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Interpreting Language Models Through Concept Descriptions: A Survey
papers.research_question: The paper surveys the field of concept descriptions for model components, aiming to answer questions about common methods and data sources, best practices for evaluation, observed trends, and key gaps and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions, charting methods, evaluation techniques, and datasets, and identifies a growing demand for rigorous causal evaluation and provides a roadmap for future research.
papers.conclusion: The use of LLMs to generate concept descriptions is a notable step towards demystifying LLMs, with a trajectory from labeling neurons to abstractions and maturing evaluation methods, but the path to verifiable causal mechanisms is not yet fully paved and costs and faithfulness concerns remain.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition of neuron polysemanticity has driven adoption of model abstractions like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and frameworks for multiple concepts per feature.
Evaluation of concept descriptions is maturing, with multi-faceted metrics assessing predictive power, input accuracy, and causal faithfulness.
The field is moving from labeling individual neurons to higher-level abstractions like SAEs and circuits.
There is a need for more rigorous causal evaluation and standardized benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Focus limited to natural language concept descriptions for internal model components and abstractions, excluding other interpretability work.
Substantial computational and financial costs associated with the methods surveyed.
Focus on English-language models and text corpora, with generalization to other languages being an open question.
future_direction: Scaling automated description methods to circuits.
Applying concept description methods to new data domains and modalities.
Analyzing the interpreters (LLMs) themselves to understand biases and limitations in generated descriptions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the decision-making processes of neural networks is a central goal of mechanistic interpretability. In the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), this involves uncovering the underlying mechanisms and identifying the roles of individual model components such as neurons and attention heads, as well as model abstractions such as the learned sparse features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). A rapidly growing line of work tackles this challenge by using powerful generator models to produce open-vocabulary, natural language concept descriptions for these components. In this paper, we provide the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions. We chart the key methods for generating these descriptions, the evolving landscape of automated and human metrics for evaluating them, and the datasets that underpin this research. Our synthesis reveals a growing demand for more rigorous, causal evaluation. By outlining the state of the art and identifying key challenges, this survey provides a roadmap for future research toward making models more transparent.

papers.title: The Logical Implication Steering Method for Conditional Interventions on Transformer Generation
papers.research_question: How to leverage concept vectors to build logical implication into pre-trained transformer models, enabling transparent and interpretable adjustments to induce generation behavior in response to concepts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Logical Implication Model Steering (LIMS) method, which uses concept vectors to program logical implication into pre-trained transformer models for interpretable behavior steering.
papers.conclusion: LIMS unlocks new hand-engineered reasoning capabilities by integrating neuro-symbolic logic into pre-trained transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
LIMS improves performance on hallucination detection, unanswerable question rejection, adversarial safety, and math reasoning tasks.
LIMS works effectively in low-data regimes (e.g., with 100 training examples).
LIMS outperforms 10-shot prompting and has advantages over DPO in interpretability and resource usage.
The method is interpretable, allowing decoupled analysis of sensing and steering components.
Mergeable LIMS (m-LIMS) performs similarly to LIMS with easier deployment but slightly reduced interpretability.
papers.limitation: The mergeable LIMS (m-LIMS) variant reduces interpretability slightly compared to standard LIMS.
future_direction: Exploring LIMS across different models or modalities.
papers.abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability in pre-trained transformer models has demonstrated substantial evidence supporting the ''linear representation hypothesis'', which is the idea that high level concepts are encoded as vectors in the space of activations of a model. Studies also show that model generation behavior can be steered toward a given concept by adding the concept's vector to the corresponding activations. We show how to leverage these properties to build a form of logical implication into models, enabling transparent and interpretable adjustments that induce a chosen generation behavior in response to the presence of any given concept. Our method, Logical Implication Model Steering (LIMS), unlocks new hand engineered reasoning capabilities by integrating neuro-symbolic logic into pre-trained transformer models.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: Why transformers are obviously good models of language
papers.research_question: Why are transformers effective models of language, and how do they align with theoretical perspectives on language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that transformers are good models of language because their architecture, such as word embeddings and attention mechanisms, aligns with cognitive linguistic theories like prototype theory and construction grammar.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are effective models of language, and their alignment with certain linguistic theories suggests that these theories, such as those from cognitive linguistics, are correct.
papers.key_findings:
Word embeddings in transformers represent prototypical meanings of words, similar to Rosch's prototype theory.
Contextualized word meanings are constructed through self-attention layers, updating prototypes based on context.
Transformers can handle syntax and top-down processing via attention heads and skip connections, analogous to construction grammar.
Transformers lack a bias for local dependencies, allowing them to learn rare long-distance dependencies effectively.
The empirical success of transformers supports cognitive linguistic approaches over traditional syntactic theories.
papers.limitation:
Transformers assert false facts with the same degree of authority as true information.
Transformers have myopia in social contexts, such as not remembering past interactions in chatbots.
papers.abstract: Nobody knows how language works, but many theories abound. Transformers are a class of neural networks that process language automatically with more success than alternatives, both those based on neural computations and those that rely on other (e.g. more symbolic) mechanisms. Here, I highlight direct connections between the transformer architecture and certain theoretical perspectives on language. The empirical success of transformers relative to alternative models provides circumstantial evidence that the linguistic approaches that transformers embody should be, at least, evaluated with greater scrutiny by the linguistics community and, at best, considered to be the currently best available theories.

papers.title: Ecco: An Open Source Library for the Explainability of Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the level of syntactic information in BERT's FFNN representations compared to hidden states, and how does syntactic information evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Ecco, an open-source library for explainability of Transformer language models, and uses it to find that syntactic information in BERT's FFNN representations is comparable to hidden states, and that hidden states build up syntactic information even when intermediate FFNNs show diminished levels.
papers.conclusion: Ecco is a tool that aids in debugging, explaining, and building intuitions about Transformer language models, and it is open-source for community contribution.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic information can be retrieved from BERT's FFNN representations at levels comparable to hidden state representations.
The model builds up syntactic information in its hidden states even when intermediate FFNNs indicate diminished levels of syntactic information.
Ecco provides tools for input saliency (gradient-based feature attribution), hidden state evolution analysis, and neuron activation analysis via dimensionality reduction and probing.
The library supports multiple explainability methods (e.g., CCA, NMF, probing) and models (GPT2, BERT, RoBERTa).
Ecco enables interactive exploration of model internals within Jupyter notebooks.
papers.limitation:
Ecco's input saliency feature is currently only supported for GPT2-based models, while neuron activation collection and dimensionality reduction are supported for GPT2, BERT, and RoBERTa.
Visualization is a starting point for building testable and falsifiable hypotheses of model interpretability, not a definitive explanation.
future_direction: Support for more models and explainability methods is under development and open for community contribution.
Future work can examine if the divergence in PoS information between FFNN and hidden states points towards layers storing different subsets of PoS information which the model assembles across layers.
papers.abstract: J Alammar. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations. 2021.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: DESTEIN: Navigating Detoxification of Language Models via Universal Steering Pairs and Head-wise Activation Fusion
papers.research_question: How can we detoxify language models efficiently with lower resource and time costs by using representation engineering in activation spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DESTEIN, a novel method for detoxifying language models via representation engineering in activation spaces using self-induced universal steering pairs and head-wise activation fusion, achieving state-of-the-art detoxification with lower computational cost while maintaining generation quality.
papers.conclusion: DESTEIN is an effective, scalable, and efficient method for detoxifying language models without fine-tuning, preserving generative capabilities and offering a new perspective for controllable generation in activation spaces.
papers.key_findings:
DESTEIN outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods in detoxification metrics (EMT and TP) while maintaining fluency and diversity.
The method is scalable across various LLMs (GPT2, LLaMA2, OPT, MPT) of different sizes.
The use of self-induced parallel steering pairs and head-wise activation fusion with probing weights is effective for detoxification.
DESTEIN exhibits a better trade-off between detoxification strength and fluency compared to previous methods, avoiding generative collapse.
The method maintains task performance on the MMLU benchmark after detoxification, similar to parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the linear representation assumption, which is an approximation and may not hold completely.
Constructing ideal parallel steering pairs is difficult.
The method is an indirect form of decoupling and faces theoretical challenges in achieving complete separation of toxic attributes and general capabilities.
future_direction: Explore more efficient and versatile decoupling strategies such as causal reasoning, knowledge guidance, or meta-learning techniques.
Integrate the method with toxicity classifiers to achieve better results by applying detoxification selectively.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable achievements of language models (LMs) across a broad spectrum of tasks, their propensity for generating toxic outputs remains a prevalent concern. Current solutions involving finetuning or auxiliary models usually require extensive computational resources, hindering their practicality in large language models (LLMs). In this paper, we propose DeStein, a novel method that detoxifies LMs by applying representation engineering in activation spaces with lower resource and time costs. Specifically, we derive detoxification vectors from self-induced, universal steering pairs through arithmetic operations in activation spaces. During inference, detoxification is achieved by fusing the detoxification vectors with the original representations in a head-wise manner. Empirical results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches on various metrics, while also maintaining satisfactory generation quality and diversity. We further validate the practicality and scalability of DeStein with a series of white-box LLMs. The method is open-sourced at https://github.com/LizLizLi/DeStein. Warning: Some example model outputs may contain highly offensive or disturbing text.

papers.title: Decomposing Natural Logic Inferences for Neural NLI
papers.research_question: Do neural NLI models capture the semantic features central to natural logic (monotonicity and concept inclusion) in their internal representations, and how does this relate to their performance on natural logic inferences?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the NLI-XY probing dataset and shows that popular NLI models lack explicit representation of context monotonicity, but fine-tuning on the HELP dataset improves both feature extractability and performance on natural logic challenge sets.
papers.conclusion: Explicit context monotonicity feature clustering in neural model representations corresponds to better performance on natural logic challenge sets, and many popular models trained on MNLI lack this behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained only on MNLI have poor performance on context monotonicity classification in their representations.
There is a correspondence between poor modeling of monotonicity features and poor performance on natural logic challenge sets.
Fine-tuning on the HELP dataset improves both the extractability of monotonicity features from representations and performance on challenge sets.
Decomposed error analysis shows models often treat downward monotone contexts as if they were upward monotone, failing to discriminate between them.
Visualization shows models fine-tuned on HELP exhibit stronger clustering of representations by context monotonicity.
papers.limitation: The permutation strategy for generating premise/hypothesis pairs may generate examples that are not consistently meaningful, which could affect the probing results.
future_direction: Investigate systematic behaviors on out-of-distribution examples generated by the permutation strategy.
papers.abstract: In the interest of interpreting neural NLI models and their reasoning strategies, we carry out a systematic probing study which investigates whether these modelscapture the crucial semantic features central to natural logic: monotonicity and concept inclusion.Correctly identifying valid inferences in downward-monotone contexts is a known stumbling block for NLI performance,subsuming linguistic phenomena such as negation scope and generalized quantifiers.To understand this difficulty, we emphasize monotonicity as a property of a context and examine the extent to which models capture relevant monotonicity information in the vector representations which are intermediate to their decision making process.Drawing on the recent advancement of the probing paradigm,we compare the presence of monotonicity features across various models.We find that monotonicity information is notably weak in the representations of popularNLI models which achieve high scores on benchmarks, and observe that previous improvements to these models based on fine-tuning strategies have introduced stronger monotonicity features together with their improved performance on challenge sets.

papers.title: Quiet Feature Learning in Algorithmic Tasks
papers.research_question: Do Transformer-based models learn meaningful internal representations (quiet features) before showing improvement in task loss, and are these features causally necessary for performance?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer-based models learn 'quiet features' (intermediate algorithmic computations) during a slow phase where task loss is stagnant, and these features are causally necessary for the subsequent sharp drop in loss.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based models encode important intermediate computations well before they show significant gains in next-token prediction, revealing a gap between internal representation learning and external task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Phase transitions occur during learning: validation loss shows a slow phase with minimal improvement followed by a fast phase of rapid decrease.
Quiet features, representing intermediate algorithmic computations, are learned during the slow phase before any decrease in task loss.
Ablation experiments show that quiet features are causally necessary for task performance.
Feature learning curves can exhibit a U-shape, where probing loss for some quiet features increases after the phase transition, suggesting representation changes.
Phase transitions are observed across different compute budgets, model sizes, dataset sizes, and within individual training runs.
future_direction: Developing theoretical frameworks to explain why models accumulate latent subroutines before observable metric improvements.
Extending the analysis to larger, more complex models and natural-language settings.
Motivating new methods for probing and monitoring internal learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: We train Transformer-based language models on ten foundational algorithmic tasks and observe pronounced phase transitions in their loss curves that deviate from established power-law scaling trends. Over large ranges of compute, the validation loss barely improves, then abruptly decreases. Probing the models' internal representations reveals that quiet features are learned prior to any decrease in task loss. These quiet features represent intermediate algorithmic computations that do not by themselves improve the output loss. Ablation experiments demonstrate that individual quiet features are causally necessary for task performance. Our results demonstrate that substantial representational progress can remain hidden beneath an apparently flat loss curve, challenging the prevailing use of cross-entropy as a proxy for learning and motivating richer diagnostics for monitoring model training.

papers.title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies the emergence of interpretable categorical features within large language models (LLMs), analyzing their behavior across training checkpoints (time), transformer layers (space), and varying model sizes (scale). Using sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, we identify when and where specific semantic concepts emerge within neural activations. Results indicate clear temporal and scale-specific thresholds for feature emergence across multiple domains. Notably, spatial analysis reveals unexpected semantic reactivation, with early-layer features re-emerging at later layers, challenging standard assumptions about representational dynamics in transformer models.

papers.title: ExpertLens: Activation steering features are highly interpretable
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether the features discovered by activation steering methods in large language models are interpretable, and if they align with human representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ExpertLens, a method based on activation steering, and shows that the expert neurons it identifies are stable across models and datasets, and their representations align closely with human conceptual structures.
papers.conclusion: ExpertLens is a flexible and lightweight approach for interpretability of LLMs, providing insights into model representations that align with human concepts.
papers.key_findings:
ExpertLens representations are stable across models and datasets.
ExpertLens representations align closely with human representations, matching inter-human alignment levels.
ExpertLens significantly outperforms the alignment captured by word/sentence embeddings.
ExpertLens can reconstruct human conceptual structure (domain organization).
Experts are learned from data, with larger models having more experts.
papers.limitation:
Only single-word concepts are considered.
Do not have access to training data.
Model choice (Pythia family).
Study neurons individually.
Polysemantic neurons are discussed.
future_direction: Future work will consider more complex concepts such as those expressing human values or preferences.
Exploration of alignment and its emergence in alternative model families.
Studying neurons jointly to capture additional aspects of concept representation.
papers.abstract: Activation steering methods in large language models (LLMs) have emerged as an effective way to perform targeted updates to enhance generated language without requiring large amounts of adaptation data. We ask whether the features discovered by activation steering methods are interpretable. We identify neurons responsible for specific concepts (e.g., ``cat'') using the ``finding experts'' method from research on activation steering and show that the ExpertLens, i.e., inspection of these neurons provides insights about model representation. We find that ExpertLens representations are stable across models and datasets and closely align with human representations inferred from behavioral data, matching inter-human alignment levels. ExpertLens significantly outperforms the alignment captured by word/sentence embeddings. By reconstructing human concept organization through ExpertLens, we show that it enables a granular view of LLM concept representation. Our findings suggest that ExpertLens is a flexible and lightweight approach for capturing and analyzing model representations.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: Can transformer language models learn positional information without explicit positional encodings, and how do they do it?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without explicit positional encodings (NoPos) can learn implicit positional information and achieve competitive performance, and this ability is due to the causal attention mask.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models can learn positional information without explicit encodings, and this phenomenon is robust across settings but does not extend to masked language models, with the causal attention mechanism being the key factor.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with explicit positional encodings across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.
Probing experiments show that NoPos models learn an implicit notion of absolute positions in their hidden representations, similar to models with learned positional embeddings.
The success of NoPos models is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Shuffling the prefix tokens leads to a dramatic increase in loss, indicating that the model uses the learned positional information.
The causal attention mask is conjectured to allow the model to infer absolute positions by counting the number of attendable tokens.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 1.3B parameters, and while the trend suggests the findings should hold for larger models, this is not tested.
NoPos models are always slightly worse than models with positional encodings, indicating that the inductive bias of positional encoding is important.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information.We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position.Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: Separating Tongue from Thought: Activation Patching Reveals Language-Agnostic Concept Representations in Transformers
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop universal concept representations that are disentangled from specific languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides causal evidence that transformer-based LLMs develop language-agnostic concept representations, as shown by activation patching experiments where averaging concept representations across languages improves translation performance.
papers.conclusion: Transformers use language-agnostic latent representations of concepts when processing word-level translation prompts, as evidenced by improved translation performance when averaging concept representations across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The model processes translation tasks by first resolving output language (layers 0-11), then the concept to be translated (layers 12-31).
Activation patching can independently manipulate language and concept information in the model's forward pass.
Patching with the mean representation of a concept across different languages improves translation performance, supporting language-agnostic representations.
These findings generalize across multiple transformer models of varying size, architecture, and training data.
The model can generate natural language descriptions of mean concept representations via activation patching.
papers.limitation: The study only considered simple concepts and did not investigate language-specific concepts.
future_direction: Improving cross-lingual transfer learning by leveraging shared concept spaces
More fine-grained probing to understand concept specialization to language
Reducing computational costs of multilingual training
papers.abstract: A central question in multilingual language modeling is whether large language models (LLMs) develop a universal concept representation, disentangled from specific languages. In this paper, we address this question by analyzing latent representations (latents) during a word-translation task in transformer-based LLMs. We strategically extract latents from a source translation prompt and insert them into the forward pass on a target translation prompt. By doing so, we find that the output language is encoded in the latent at an earlier layer than the concept to be translated. Building on this insight, we conduct two key experiments. First, we demonstrate that we can change the concept without changing the language and vice versa through activation patching alone. Second, we show that patching with the mean representation of a concept across different languages does not affect the models' ability to translate it, but instead improves it. Finally, we generalize to multi-token generation and demonstrate that the model can generate natural language description of those mean representations. Our results provide evidence for the existence of language-agnostic concept representations within the investigated models.

papers.title: Towards Understanding How Transformers Learn In-context Through a Representation Learning Lens
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) in Transformers work? Can ICL be related to gradient descent under the softmax attention setting without specific constructions for model weights and input tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the ICL inference process of a softmax attention layer is equivalent to gradient descent on a dual model, provides a representation learning interpretation, derives a generalization bound, and proposes attention modifications inspired by contrastive learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that ICL can be understood as gradient descent on a dual model from a representation learning perspective, and that attention modifications inspired by this view show promise in enhancing model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The ICL inference of a softmax attention layer is equivalent to one step of gradient descent on a dual model with a loss function that maximizes similarity between value-projected and key-projected tokens.
The dual model's training resembles a self-supervised representation learning process, analogous to contrastive learning without negative samples.
A generalization error bound for ICL is derived, showing the error decreases with the number of demonstration tokens.
The equivalence extends to a full Transformer layer (with FFN) and multiple attention layers.
Attention modifications inspired by representation learning (regularization, data augmentation, negative samples) can improve model performance on synthetic and GLUE tasks.
papers.limitation:
The negative sample selection method is too coarse and not always effective.
The attention modifications are tested on limited tasks and may not generalize.
future_direction: Develop more task-specific augmentation strategies for attention.
Design more effective methods for constructing negative samples in the attention mechanism.
Apply the representation learning lens to other model components and settings.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large language models based on Transformers have demonstrated remarkable in-context learning (ICL) abilities. With just a few demonstration examples, the models can implement new tasks without any parameter updates. However, it is still an open question to understand the mechanism of ICL. In this paper, we attempt to explore the ICL process in Transformers through a lens of representation learning. Initially, leveraging kernel methods, we figure out a dual model for one softmax attention layer. The ICL inference process of the attention layer aligns with the training procedure of its dual model, generating token representation predictions that are equivalent to the dual model's test outputs. We delve into the training process of this dual model from a representation learning standpoint and further derive a generalization error bound related to the quantity of demonstration tokens. Subsequently, we extend our theoretical conclusions to more complicated scenarios, including one Transformer layer and multiple attention layers. Furthermore, drawing inspiration from existing representation learning methods especially contrastive learning, we propose potential modifications for the attention layer. Finally, experiments are designed to support our findings.

papers.title: How Do Vision Transformers Work?
papers.research_question: How do multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) work? Specifically, what properties of MSAs improve optimization, how do MSAs differ from convolutional layers (Convs), and how can we harmonize MSAs with Convs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that MSAs in Vision Transformers act as generalized spatial smoothing, flattening loss landscapes and improving generalization, and are complementary to convolutional layers as low-pass vs. high-pass filters. Based on these insights, the paper proposes AlterNet, a model that alternates Conv and MSA blocks, which outperforms CNNs even on small datasets.
papers.conclusion: MSAs are generalized spatial smoothings that complement Convs, and harmonizing them via an alternating pattern leads to models that outperform CNNs across data regimes.
papers.key_findings:
MSAs improve accuracy and generalization by flattening loss landscapes, primarily due to data specificity rather than long-range dependency.
MSAs are low-pass filters that reduce high-frequency signals and aggregate feature maps, while Convs are high-pass filters that amplify high-frequency signals and diversify feature maps.
ViTs suffer from non-convex losses in small data regimes, which can be alleviated by large datasets or loss landscape smoothing methods.
Multi-stage neural networks behave like series connections of small individual models, and MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction.
The proposed AlterNet, which alternates Conv and MSA blocks, outperforms CNNs not only on large datasets but also on small datasets.
papers.limitation: The effects of data augmentation on loss landscapes and uncertainty calibration require further investigation.
future_direction: Further investigation into the effects of data augmentation on uncertainty calibration and loss landscapes.
papers.abstract: The success of multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) for computer vision is now indisputable. However, little is known about how MSAs work. We present fundamental explanations to help better understand the nature of MSAs. In particular, we demonstrate the following properties of MSAs and Vision Transformers (ViTs): (1) MSAs improve not only accuracy but also generalization by flattening the loss landscapes. Such improvement is primarily attributable to their data specificity, not long-range dependency. On the other hand, ViTs suffer from non-convex losses. Large datasets and loss landscape smoothing methods alleviate this problem; (2) MSAs and Convs exhibit opposite behaviors. For example, MSAs are low-pass filters, but Convs are high-pass filters. Therefore, MSAs and Convs are complementary; (3) Multi-stage neural networks behave like a series connection of small individual models. In addition, MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction. Based on these insights, we propose AlterNet, a model in which Conv blocks at the end of a stage are replaced with MSA blocks. AlterNet outperforms CNNs not only in large data regimes but also in small data regimes. The code is available at https://github.com/xxxnell/how-do-vits-work.

papers.title: What Does BERT Look at? An Analysis of BERT’s Attention
papers.research_question: What specific linguistic features does BERT learn from unlabeled data, as revealed by its attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's attention heads capture syntactic and coreference information, and proposes methods for analyzing attention mechanisms to reveal this linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Attention maps contain substantial linguistic knowledge and complement other model analysis techniques, and should be part of the toolkit for understanding what neural networks learn about language.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads exhibit common patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence.
Certain attention heads specialize to specific syntactic relations (e.g., direct objects, determiners) with high accuracy.
One attention head performs well at coreference resolution.
An attention-based probing classifier achieves 77 UAS on dependency parsing, showing BERT's attention captures substantial syntactic information.
Attention heads in the same layer tend to behave similarly.
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.

papers.title: Multi-Head Attention: Collaborate Instead of Concatenate
papers.research_question: How redundant are the key/query projections in multi-head attention, and can we design a more parameter-efficient multi-head attention mechanism by sharing these projections?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes collaborative multi-head attention, which shares key/query projections across heads, reducing parameters without performance loss and enabling post-hoc compression of pre-trained models.
papers.conclusion: Collaborative multi-head attention is a more efficient alternative to concatenation-based multi-head attention, reducing redundancy and enabling parameter reduction without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Heads in standard multi-head attention learn redundant key/query projections, as shown by PCA.
Collaborative attention can reduce the key/query dimension by 4x without performance drop in NMT and vision tasks.
Pre-trained models can be re-parametrized into collaborative attention via tensor decomposition, allowing compression without retraining.
Collaborative attention consistently improves over concatenation-based attention with the same number of parameters.
The method is effective across modalities (text and image) and various transformer architectures (BERT, DistilBERT, ALBERT, DeiT).
papers.limitation: ALBERT suffers more from compression, possibly because it already shares parameters across layers, which may limit the redundancy that can be exploited.
papers.abstract: Attention layers are widely used in natural language processing (NLP) and are beginning to influence computer vision architectures. Training very large transformer models allowed significant improvement in both fields, but once trained, these networks show symptoms of over-parameterization. For instance, it is known that many attention heads can be pruned without impacting accuracy. This work aims to enhance current understanding on how multiple heads interact. Motivated by the observation that attention heads learn redundant key/query projections, we propose a collaborative multi-head attention layer that enables heads to learn shared projections. Our scheme decreases the number of parameters in an attention layer and can be used as a drop-in replacement in any transformer architecture. Our experiments confirm that sharing key/query dimensions can be exploited in language understanding, machine translation and vision. We also show that it is possible to re-parametrize a pre-trained multi-head attention layer into our collaborative attention layer. Collaborative multi-head attention reduces the size of the key and query projections by 4 for same accuracy and speed. Our code is public.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that input perturbations reveal how transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and that such perturbations are a useful analysis tool for interpreting deep language models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and attention changes partially explain this sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing context scale along layers.
Swapping phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrases, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, especially in deeper layers.
Attention changes partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance.
The distortion metric correlates with impairment of syntactic probes (POS, grandparent tags, tree distance).
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features.
Searching for causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance.
Applying perturbation analyses to models trained on shuffled data or models with explicit syntax.
papers.abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure. Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for interpreting complex black-box models. 1

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: Revisiting Out-of-Distribution Generalization in NLI Models
papers.research_question: Does poor performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets truly indicate a lack of knowledge, or is it a symptom of misalignment between the encoder’s representations and the classifier’s decision boundaries?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that despite poor classifier accuracy on out-of-distribution NLI datasets, the encoder's representations remain highly linearly separable, indicating that the encoder captures task-relevant knowledge that the classifier head fails to exploit due to misaligned decision boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The encoder in NLI models acquires core linguistic knowledge that generalizes beyond the training distribution, but poor OOD accuracy arises from a misalignment between the classifier's decision boundaries and the encoder's representations.
papers.key_findings:
Encoder representations for OOD datasets (e.g., HANS, Stress Test) show near-perfect linear separability even when classifier accuracy is poor or random.
Linear separability of OOD data improves with more training data and iterations, correlating with the model's acquisition of task knowledge.
Balancing the training dataset to remove lexical overlap bias does not improve model performance on HANS, suggesting the bias is not solely due to overlap heuristics.
Instability in OOD generalization across random seeds stems from the classifier head's sensitivity to initialization, not from the encoder's representations, which remain consistent.
For some OOD datasets (e.g., ST-NU), linear separability is very high (>95%) despite low classifier accuracy, indicating the encoder effectively captures necessary information.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was limited to three pretrained language models (DistilBERT, BERT, RoBERTa), so findings may not generalize to newer or more specialized models.
The study does not provide a direct solution for improving classification accuracy on OOD datasets.
Relying on linear separability as a proxy for model knowledge may oversimplify the complexity of how models truly understand inference.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how well discriminative transformers generalize in Natural Language Inference (NLI) tasks.We specifically focus on a well-studied bias in this task: the tendency of models to rely on superficial features and dataset biases rather than a true understanding of language.We argue that the performance differences observed between training and analysis datasets do not necessarily indicate a lack of knowledge within the model.Instead, the gap often points to a misalignment between the decision boundaries of the classifier head and the representations learned by the encoder for the analysis samples.By investigating the representation space of NLI models across different analysis datasets, we demonstrate that even when the accuracy is nearly random in some settings, still samples from opposing classes remain almost perfectly linearly separable in the encoder's representation space.This suggests that, although the classifier head may fail on analysis data, the encoder still generalizes and encodes representations that allow for effective discrimination between NLI classes.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Learning Syntax Without Planting Trees: Understanding Hierarchical Generalization in Transformers
papers.research_question: Why do transformers show hierarchical generalization, despite lacking architectural biases towards hierarchical structure?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the language modeling objective consistently leads transformers to generalize hierarchically on synthetic tasks, and provides a Bayesian explanation linking this preference to the simplicity of hierarchical grammars.
papers.conclusion: The language modeling objective is a key inductive bias for hierarchical generalization in transformers, and a Bayesian perspective explains this preference via the simplicity of hierarchical grammars.
papers.key_findings:
The language modeling objective consistently leads to hierarchical generalization across five synthetic tasks, while other objectives like sequence-to-sequence modeling often fail.
Subnetworks implementing hierarchical and linear generalizations coexist within the trained transformer and persist throughout training.
The coexistence of subnetworks is due to ambiguous training data; adding disambiguating examples causes the linear subnetwork to disappear.
A Bayesian analysis shows that transformers generalize hierarchically when hierarchical grammars have higher posterior probability than regular grammars, indicating a preference for simpler explanations.
In a low-diversity dataset where regular grammars have higher posterior, transformers fail to generalize hierarchically, confirming the correlation.
papers.limitation:
The study only considers synthetic datasets and small transformer models; it is unclear if findings extend to larger models trained on natural language corpora.
The Bayesian analysis relies on hand-constructed grammars and specific prior choices; while sensitivity analysis is performed, other priors could lead to different conclusions.
The pruning method only considers attention heads; other components like MLPs are not included.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to larger transformer models trained on natural language corpora.
Include other model components beyond attention heads in pruning and analysis.
Apply the Bayesian framework to study other forms of generalization in language models.
papers.abstract: Transformers trained on natural language data have been shown to learn its hierarchical structure and generalize to sentences with unseen syntactic structures without explicitly encoding any structural bias. In this work, we investigate sources of inductive bias in transformer models and their training that could cause such generalization behavior to emerge. We extensively experiment with transformer models trained on multiple synthetic datasets and with different training objectives and show that while other objectives e.g. sequence-to-sequence modeling, prefix language modeling, often failed to lead to hierarchical generalization, models trained with the language modeling objective consistently learned to generalize hierarchically. We then conduct pruning experiments to study how transformers trained with the language modeling objective encode hierarchical structure. When pruned, we find joint existence of subnetworks within the model with different generalization behaviors (subnetworks corresponding to hierarchical structure and linear order). Finally, we take a Bayesian perspective to further uncover transformers' preference for hierarchical generalization: We establish a correlation between whether transformers generalize hierarchically on a dataset and whether the simplest explanation of that dataset is provided by a hierarchical grammar compared to regular grammars exhibiting linear generalization.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
